Mouzi was a Confucian scholar from Cangwu who lived after [Mou] Rong. He flourished during the second year of the Xingping era of Emperor Xian (254 CE).

Because the world was in turmoil, he had no intention of seeking office. Resolute in his commitment to the Buddhist Way, he composed the *Lihuolun* (Treatise on Dispelling Doubts) in thirty-seven chapters.
In its text, there is a question that asks: "Why is the Buddha correctly called 'Buddha'? What does 'Buddha' mean? Mouzi replied: "Buddha means 'awakening.
It is like the Three Sovereigns being divine and the Five Emperors being sagely. The Buddha is the primordial ancestor of the Way and its Virtue, and of spiritual intelligence."
The lineage of the school: That which the Buddha calls "Awakening" is a state of mystical transformation. It can divide its body and disperse its form; it may appear to exist or vanish;
it can become small or large, round or square, old or young; it can remain hidden or manifest. Treading upon fire, it is not burned;

walking upon blades, it is not wounded; dwelling in filth, it is not defiled; encountering calamity, it is not afflicted. It reaches its destination without traveling; it shines forth without acting. Therefore—
He is titled "Buddha. A questioner asked: "Now, the ultimate reality is not flowery, and the ultimate words are not embellished. Pearls and jade are rare and thus precious;
tiles and pebbles are abundant and thus base. When the Sages composed the root texts of the Seven Classics, they did not exceed thirty thousand words, yet all matters were complete therein."
"Currently, the Buddhist scriptures number in the tens of thousands; their words are counted by the hundreds of millions. This is beyond the capacity of a single person to master.
I consider them cumbersome and lacking in essential meaning. Mouzi replied: "The reason the rivers and seas differ from puddles in the road is that they are deep and vast.
The reason the Five Peaks distinguish themselves from mere hills is that they are high and great. If they were not high..."
Mountains and hills are impassable, yet the lame sheep climbs to their summits; the depths are so profound that not even a trickle flows through, yet the young child bathes in their abyss.

The qilin does not dwell within the confines of a garden, and the fish that swallows a boat does not swim in a stream only several *ren* deep. Why is this? It is because the small cannot contain the great.
The Buddhist scriptures speak of events from billions of years past and describe the essentials for ten thousand generations to come. This is the Great Primal Simplicity (*tai su*).
It has not yet arisen; it has not yet been born in the Great Beginning (*tai-shi*). Its subtlety cannot be grasped; its fineness cannot be entered.

The Buddha has completely encompassed that which lies beyond the vast and has analyzed that which dwells within the profound. There is nothing he does not record; thus his scriptures number in the tens of thousands and his words reach into the hundreds of millions.
The more there are, the more complete they become; the more numerous they are, the more abundant they grow. How could there be anything omitted?

Question: The Buddha-way is most supreme and most great. Why did Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius not cultivate it? It is not seen in the words of the Seven Classics. Since you are already devoted to the Odes and Documents and take pleasure in the Rites and Music, why do you further favor the Buddha-way? I privately believe that you, my son, should not adopt it. Mouzi replied: Books are not necessarily the words of Confucius; medicine is not necessarily that of Bian Que. The Way is simply what is right. If one can attain the Way, why must it be through Confucius? If one can cure illness, why must it be through Bian Que? If one can reach the truth, why must it be through the Six Classics? If one can achieve the goal, why must it be through the Hundred Schools? Therefore, although the Buddha-way is profound and subtle, it is not necessarily superior to the teachings of the Sages. Although the Six Classics are vast and extensive, they are not necessarily superior to the Buddha-way. If one does not examine the principles but merely disputes the names, this is like a blind man who, when shown a jewel, says he does not believe in its existence because he cannot see it. If one does not investigate the meaning but merely disputes the words, this is like a deaf person who, when told of music, says he does not believe in its existence because he cannot hear it. If one does not seek the essence but merely disputes the form, this is like a hungry person who, when offered food, says he does not believe in its existence because he has not eaten it. If one does not practice the virtue but merely disputes the doctrine, this is like a cold person who, when given fire, says he does not believe in its existence because he has not warmed himself. Thus, if one examines the principles and investigates the meaning, the Buddha-way is indeed superior. If one seeks the essence and practices the virtue, the Buddha-way is indeed great. If one merely disputes the names and words without examining the principles and investigating the meaning, this is like a blind man disputing colors, a deaf person disputing sounds, a hungry person disputing flavors, a cold person disputing warmth, or a person with no knowledge disputing the Way. How can such a person be called wise? Therefore, I say: books are not necessarily the words of Confucius; medicine is not necessarily that of Bian Que. The Way is simply what is right. If one can attain the Way, why must it be through Confucius? If one can cure illness, why must it be through Bian Que? If one can reach the truth, why must it be through the Six Classics? If one can achieve the goal, why must it be through the Hundred Schools? This is why I favor the Buddha-way. It is not that I am biased against the teachings of the Sages. It is simply that I wish to clarify the truth. If one truly understands the truth, one will naturally respect the Sages. If one truly knows the Way, one will naturally honor the Buddha. This is like a traveler who, having reached his destination, naturally respects the guide; or like a sick person who, having been cured, naturally honors the physician. As for this method: those who join in deliberation will follow it; those who apply it to their ailments will find it excellent. A gentleman extensively adopts the many virtues of others to assist his own person.
Zigong said, "What constant teachers does the Master have? Yao served Yǐn Shòu; Shùn served Wùchéng;

Dàn studied under Lǚ Wàng; and Kūngxiū studied under Lǎo Tán. These matters are not fully recorded in the Seven Classics. How much more so regarding the transformation of the Buddha’s body and its marks of excellence?
Transformation is such that its spiritual powers are boundless; how could one abandon them and fail to study them?

As for the matters and meanings of the Five Classics, there are some deficiencies that the Buddha did not record—what is there to be surprised about? It is asked: "The Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics."

"How extraordinary they are, compared to ordinary people! This is likely the talk of those whose ears are filled with wealth; it is not a statement of reality. Mōuzi replied: "Those who have seen little marvel at what is much.
Upon seeing a camel, one says a horse has a swollen back. Yao had eyebrows of eight colors; Shun had double pupils; Gāoyáo had a bird-like beak;
King Wén had four nipples; Yǔ had three openings in his ears; Zhōu Gong had a hunched back; and Fúxī was dragon-shaped."
The nose of Zhongni (Confucius) was arched; Laozi had a sun-like mark on his forehead and deep-set eyes, with two pillars on his nose, ten lines on his palms, and two sets of five marks on his feet.
Is this not different from ordinary men? Why then should one doubt the *lakṣaṇas* and *anuvyañjanas* of the Buddha? Question:
You employ the language of the classics and commentaries, and use flowery rhetoric to praise the Buddha’s conduct and extol his virtue, making it so lofty that it surpasses the azure heavens.
Yun said: "To expand [the teachings] so that they exceed the boundaries of the earth—is this not to surpass their original foundation and exceed their true measure? Mouzi replied: "Alas!
My praise is like adding a speck of dust to Mount Song or Mount Dai, or gathering the morning dew and casting it into the vast ocean. As for your censure,"
It is like grasping a ladle or a gourd while wishing to diminish the rivers and seas; or wielding a plow while wishing to erode Mount Kunlun.

It is like holding up a single fist to shield out the sun, or lifting a clod of earth to block the current of a river. My praise cannot make the Buddha higher, nor can your disparagement cause him to fall lower.
Cao Zhi was profoundly skilled in the arts of calligraphy; Han Dan Chun praised him as being "Heavenly."
Whenever he read Buddhist scriptures, he would linger over them, sighing in admiration and playing with the text, regarding them as the ultimate pinnacle of the Supreme Way.
Once, while traveling at Mount Yushan, he heard the sound of Brahma in the sky—clear, resonant, and plaintively beautiful—and thus modeled his own voice after it to compose *fanbai* (Brahma-chants).

The current ritual practice includes the *Yushan* (Fishing Mountain) *fan* (chanting), which is a remnant of those musical performances. He once composed the "Discourse on Distinguishing the Dao" (*Bian dao lun*), in which he argued that the Way of the Immortals is empty and false.

According to the biography of Liu Yao in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, Yao traveled up the Yangtze River southward to take refuge in Yuzhang, stationing his forces at Pengze; there, Ze Rong had already arrived beforehand.
He killed the Governor Zhu Hao and took up residence in the commandery. When Zhang Rong advanced to attack him, he was defeated by Rong;

however, he subsequently recruited forces from the subordinate counties and defeated Rong. Rong fled into the mountains and was killed by the local populace. Zhang Rong died shortly thereafter from illness at the age of forty-two.
As for Ze Rong, he was a native of Danyang who initially gathered several hundred followers and went to seek refuge with the Governor of Xuzhou.

Tao Qian. Qian was appointed by [the Emperor] to supervise the transport of grain to Guangling and Pengcheng; he subsequently became licentious and acted with arbitrary authority, executing people at will.

He intercepted the official supplies from the three commanderies to enrich himself. He then constructed a grand Buddhist temple, fashioning human figures out of copper and gilding their bodies with gold.

They were dressed in brocade and embroidery, and hung with nine tiers of copper basins. Below, there were multi-storied pavilions and walkways capable of accommodating more than three thousand people.
He established a requirement for all to recite Buddhist scriptures and permitted those within his jurisdiction and neighboring districts who were devoted to the Buddha to receive the Way.
Furthermore, he remitted other corvée labor to attract them. Consequently, from near and far, over five thousand people arrived, one after another.
Every time the Buddha was bathed, the household would provide abundant wine and rice, spreading mats along the road for several tens of *li*. The common people came to witness the event, and...

The number of those who took up residence there reached ten thousand, and the expenses were calculated in the hundreds of millions. When Cao Gong attacked Tao Qian, the region of Xu was thrown into turmoil.
Rong led ten thousand men and women and three thousand horses to Guangling. Zhao Yu, the Governor of Guangling, received him with the courtesy due to a guest.
Previously, Xue Li, the Chancellor of Pengcheng, had been pressed by Tao Qian and was stationed at Moling; Rong found Guangling advantageous.

Sun Ling’s forces took advantage of the terrain to execute Sun Yü. They unleashed their troops on a large-scale raid, carrying him away; they passed through and killed Sun Li, and only then did they kill Sun Hào.
According to the *Fofa jintang bian*, Kan Ze was a native of Shanyin, Kuaiji. He was fond of learning but lived in poverty, working as a copyist for others.

He was self-sufficient. Once he had finished copying a text, he was able to recite it from memory. Through this means, he read extensively across various scriptures. When Yu Fan saw him, he praised him, saying:
"Kǎn Shēng is a man of exceptional talent; he is the successor to Zhōngshū and Zǐyún. Sūn Quán summoned him for service, appointing him as a Censor of the Western Office (Xīcáo Yuàn).

He was subsequently enfeoffed as the Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifǔ) and appointed as the Minister of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng), with the title of Marquis of Dūxiāng. He once donated his residence to establish a temple of virtue.
Regarding Run Temple: Quan once asked, "Confucius composed the classic teachings to instruct future generations;

Laozi and Zhuangzi cultivated their persons for self-delight and wandered freely among mountains and waters, setting their hearts upon tranquility. Why, then, would they have recourse to Buddhism? Ze replied, "The two teachings of Confucius and Laozi..."
The laws of Heaven establish their functions; one dares not disobey Heaven. The Buddha established his teachings; all the devas receive and uphold them; they dare not disobey the Buddha.
From this it may be seen that the relative superiority and inferiority [of the two] are evident.
From the *Qi Chunqiu*: Prince Zimo of Jin’an, courtesy name Yunchang, was the son of Emperor Wu. When he was seven years old, his mother, Lady Ruan Shuyuan, fell gravely ill.
He requested monks to perform religious rites. There was one who offered lotus flowers as an offering to the Buddha;

the assembly of monks placed them in a copper pitcher filled with water, and the flowers became even more vibrant. Prince Zimo wept as he prostrated before the Buddha and made this vow: "If my aunt..."
May you grant protection. I pray that the flowers may remain as they were until the end of the fast. When the seven-day fast was completed, the flowers were even more fresh and crimson than before.
Looking into the jar, there were already some roots and filaments. Yuan’s illness soon abated; the world praised this as an instance of filial piety moving Heaven.
From the *Book of Jin*, the biography of Zhou Jun: Zhou Jun’s son, Song, was appointed as Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief.
Wang Dun secretly dispatched the sorcerer Li Tuo to falsely accuse Song and Zhou Yan of conspiring to secretly appoint officials; he subsequently had them executed. Song was devoted to Buddhism;
even at the moment of his execution, he continued to recite sutras in the marketplace.
From the Biography of Cai Mo: Prince Pengcheng Tong submitted a memorial stating that in the Le Xian Hall there was a Buddhist image painted by the late Emperor’s own hand;

though it had endured the hardships of successive rebellions, this hall still remained. He suggested that an edict be issued to compose a eulogy for it. The Emperor put the matter before his ministers for discussion. Cai Mo said:

"Buddhism is a custom of the barbarians and not a system established by the Classics. The late Emperor’s capacity was equal to Heaven and Earth, and he possessed manifold talents and arts; [he merely]..."
This image was painted on a temporary basis; as for [the Emperor’s] refined devotion to the Buddha-way, we have not heard of it before.
Amidst the sudden onset of bandits and the ruin of the royal capital, this hall alone remains standing in its entirety. This is truly a sign that divine spirits are protecting and blessing it.
However, it does not yet constitute a full representation of the magnificent virtue of the Great Jin, nor is it the primary subject for songs of praise. When a minister beholds...
"Things arise according to their inherent principles; it would be appropriate for a private person to compose a fu or a song of praise.

However, I now wish to issue an imperial decree to the court historians to extol the late Emperor’s devotion to Buddhism above, and to compose a hymn for the Buddha image for the sake of the barbarians below. I have doubts regarding the propriety of this matter, and thus I have let the proposal lie."

The Biography of Wang Xun. Xun’s younger brother, Wang Min, surpassed Xun in reputation. At that time, there was a foreign śramaṇa named Deva, who possessed a profound understanding of the principles of the Dharma.
He lectured on the *Abhidharma* Sūtra for the two brothers. Min was still quite young at the time; before the lecture had even reached its halfway point, he remarked:

Having understood it, he immediately went to a separate room and lectured on it himself with several people, including Famen and Fagang. Fagang sighed in admiration, saying, "The great meanings are all correct;
it is only that the minor details have not yet been refined."
According to the *Zhongzhuan*: When Emperor Mu ascended the throne, He Chong held the reins of government and summoned Sengzhong again to serve as Commander-in-Chief (*lingjun*).

Sengzhong did not accept the appointment; he only took office after his period of mourning had ended. At that time, He Chong was on bad terms with Prince of Wuling, but Sengzhong mediated between them, whereby they were finally reconciled.

He Chong held Buddhism in high esteem and placed great faith in it, while Sengzhong discussed its wasteful expenditures, frequently voicing these criticisms. Once, he traveled in the same carriage with He Chong.

When passing through Buddhist temples, He Chong would enter with his retinue; the others did not dismount from their carriages, yet Chong, on account of his status as a prominent elder of the state and the local community, always treated them with exceptional courtesy.

According to the *Biography of He Chong*, Chong was by nature fond of the Buddhist scriptures and devoted himself to the construction and repair of Buddhist temples, providing for hundreds of śramaṇas at his own expense.

He spent billions without any sense of parsimony, yet when it came to his relatives and friends who were impoverished, he had nothing to bestow upon them; for this reason, he incurred criticism from the world.
Once, Ruan Yu teased him, saying, "Your ambitions are as vast as the universe, and your courage surpasses that of all ages.

When Wang Chong asked him the reason for this, Yu replied, "I was planning to obtain a commandery of several thousand households, yet I have not even been able to achieve that. You, however, plan to become a Buddha—is that not so?"

"How great it is! At that time, Xi Yin and his younger brother Tan followed the Way of the Celestial Master (Tianshi Dao), whereas Fu Chong and his younger brother Zhun venerated and placed their faith in the Śākya clan (Buddhism).
Xie Wan criticized them, saying: "The two Xi brothers are sycophants toward the Dao; the two He brothers are flatterers toward the Buddha."
The Biography of He Zhun. Zhun’s courtesy name was Youdao; he was the father of Empress Mu Zhang. Noble-minded and possessing few desires, he became renowned by the age of twenty.

Although both the provincial and the metropolitan governments issued summons for him, he did not accept either. His elder brother, He Chong, served as General of the Flying Cavalry (Biaoji Jiangjun) and urged him to take office.
Zhun replied, "How could the fifth rank be inferior to that of a General of the Flying Cavalry? This remark arose because Zhun was the fifth among his brothers; thus spoke Chong.
While those in the high positions of prime ministers and ministers wielded power that dominated their era, Zǔn wore his sash loosely at his humble gate, withdrew from worldly affairs,
and devoted himself solely to reciting Buddhist scriptures and constructing pagodas and temples.
In the *Fofa Jintang Bian* (Compilation on the Golden Fortifications of the Buddha-Dharma), it is recorded that Xi Chao served as a secretary in the administration of Huan Wen.
Xi Chao asked Xie An, "How does the discourse of Zhi Dun compare to that of Xi Kang? An replied, "Xi Kang exhausted his powers of reasoning, yet he only attained half [the truth].

Xi Chao then composed a text on the Five Precepts and further cultivated the practice of monthly and seasonal fasting and purification. During these fasts, he was not permitted to taste fish or meat, nor did he consort with his wife or concubines; he would welcome the arrival of noon [to begin the rites].
He ate [the food], but after he had finished eating, he could not taste its delicious flavor or fragrance at all; he purified his mind to contemplate the Way and took refuge in the Three Realities.
According to the *Book of Jin*, Biography of Wang Zan: Zan’s grandson was Shu, and Shu’s son was Tanzhi, who maintained very close ties with the śramaṇa Zhu Fashi. Every time...
They discussed together the mysteries of the world beyond and the retribution of karmic cause and effect, stipulating that the one who died first should report on these matters.

After a year had passed, the Master suddenly arrived and said, "I, this poor monk, have already died. Both sin and merit are never in vain; one must simply diligently cultivate the Way and its Virtue in order to elevate and deliver the spiritual intelligence.
Having finished speaking, he vanished. Zhan Tan soon thereafter also passed away.
From the *Biography of Fotudeng*: When Shi Jilong usurped the throne, he devoted himself entirely to Fotudeng. Because of Fotudeng, many among the common people came to revere the Buddha;
they all constructed temples and vied with one another to leave the household life. Consequently, the genuine and the false became intermingled, and many committed transgressions.

Shi Jilong issued an edict to investigate and distinguish between them. His Court Historian Wang Du submitted a memorial stating: "The Buddha is the deity of a foreign land; he is not [a deity] of the Chinese."

Regarding those who should be worshipped and served: when the Way was first transmitted during the Han dynasty, it was permitted only for people from the Western Regions to establish monasteries in the capital cities to serve their deities;
Han people were not permitted to leave the household life at all. The Wei dynasty inherited the Han system and likewise followed these precedents.

Now, you may decree that none of the people of Zhao shall be permitted to go to monasteries to burn incense or prostrate, so as to adhere to the rites and ceremonies. As for the various high officials and ministers...
Scholars and even common slaves were all prohibited from doing so by precedent. Those who violated this were punished with the same penalty as those guilty of illicit worship at heterodox shrines.

As for those among the people of Zhao who had become śramaṇas, they were ordered to return to lay life. Many court officials concurred with the proposal. Because of Fotudeng, Shi Le issued an edict stating:
"I am of a frontier barbarian origin and have unworthily ruled over the Central Lands. Regarding sacrifices and offerings, one should follow the customs of one's own origins."

The Buddha is a deity of the Rong people; one should also serve his [the Buddha's] followers. Wang Zhao permitted those among the common people who delighted in serving the Buddha to do so specifically.
According to the *Biography of Wang Gong*: When Gong was about to flee from Huan Yuan, he reached Changtang Lake and encountered a merchant named Qian Qiang, who informed him [of the situation].
The Magistrate of Hupou arrested him and sent him to the capital. He was executed at Nitang in Jiankang. [Zhu] Gong had faith in Buddhism and Daoism;
when he conscripted the common people to repair and construct Buddhist temples, his primary concern was their magnificence. Consequently, the gentry and commoners resented and lamented him.
Even as he faced execution, he continued to recite Buddhist scriptures and said to the executioner: "I was deluded in my trust of others, which led me to this."
From the *Fú Jiān Zǎi Jì* (Annals of Fú Jiān): While Fú Jiān was strolling in the Eastern Garden, he ordered the śramaṇa Dào’ān to share his carriage. Quán Yì remonstrated, saying:

"I have heard that when the Son of Heaven travels in full imperial procession, the Zhōngshì (Attendant-in-Ordinary) accompanies him in the carriage, clearing the way as they proceed with regulated movements.

Even the last rulers of the Three Dynasties might have violated the great ethical relations for the sake of a temporary sentiment, yet their misconduct was recorded for posterity. Thus, Bān Jī declined to ride in the carriage."
The resulting beauty was boundless. Dao’an, a man of humble status who had disfigured his body for the sake of the Way, felt it inappropriate to defile the divine palanquin.

Fu Jian changed countenance and said, “Master An’s public virtue reaches the ultimate realm, and his merit is honored by the age. Though I were to offer the entire weight of the empire, it would not suffice to exchange it for him.
This is no mere honor for you to be carried in a palanquin; rather, it is my own manifest glory. He then ordered attendants to support Dao’an as he ascended the palanquin.
The Record of Yao Xing’s Reign: Yao Xing devoted his mind to Buddhism and Daoism; from the high officials down to the commoners, there were none who did not revere and follow him.
Over five thousand śramaṇas arrived from afar. He erected a stūpa in Yonggui Li and established a Prajñā Terrace within the inner palace.

Śramaṇas practicing dhyāna seated meditation numbered constantly in the thousands. Throughout the provinces and commanderies, those who were transformed by his influence and served the Buddha reached ten [thousand].
This makes nine instances in the chamber.

According to the *Sou Shen Hou Ji* (Sequel to the Records of Searching for Spirits), Hu Maohui of Huainan during the Jin dynasty was able to see ghosts; though he did not like seeing them, he could not stop himself.
Later, while traveling to Yangzhou, he returned to Linyang City. To the east there was a shrine where a local official happened to be accompanied by a shamaness.
They performed a sacrificial offering. After a short while, a group of ghosts shouted to one another, "The high official is coming! and they each fled from the shrine.
Looking back, they saw two śramaṇas entering the shrine; the ghosts, in groups of twos and threes, huddled together and waited in the grass by the shrine.
Upon seeing the śramaṇas, they were all struck with fear. In a moment, the two śramaṇas...
He departed through the gate. Afterwards, all the ghosts returned to the shrine. Thereupon, Sengmao believed in the Buddha and consequently served the Dharma with sincere devotion.
[From] the *Fofa Jintang Bian* (Compendium of the Buddhist Dharma as a Moat and Rampart). Gu Kaizhi, courtesy name Changkang, childhood name Houtou, was skilled in painting.

He was recruited by Huan Wen as a military aide (*sima canjun*). At that time, the śramaṇa Huili was constructing Waguan Temple; among the court elites who offered donations, there were none—[who did not do so].
