Biography of Liu Xiao. Xiao maintained a life of purity and frugality, having no personal indulgences. By nature, he did not boast of his own virtues nor discuss the merits or faults of others.

Upon encountering the Buddhist scriptures and teachings, he constantly practiced compassion and forbearance. In the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era, following the death of his mother, he permanently abstained from meat and pungent flavors, observing the fasts and subsisting on vegetarian food.
When he approached his end, he left a final testament that he be enshrouded in monastic robes and carried [in a funeral palanquin].
They used an open carriage to return the remains for burial in the old cemetery; they secured whatever plot of land was available, sufficient only to contain the coffin.
They were not permitted to set up an ancestral altar or offer sacrificial libations. His son followed this practice.
The Biography of Teng Tanguang. Tanguang was a native of Nanchang in Yuzhang. When he was five years old, his mother, Lady Yang, suffered from a fever and longed for cold melons.
As these were not produced in the local customs of that region, Tanguang searched everywhere, yet could not obtain any. He was consumed by intense grief.
Suddenly, he encountered a śramaṇa who asked him the reason for his actions. Tanguo related the matter in detail, whereupon the śramaṇa said, "I have two melons;
let me give you one as a gift. Tanguo bowed in thanks and, carrying the melon back home, offered it to his mother. The entire household was struck with wonder and amazement.
He searched for the śramaṇa, but did not know his whereabouts. When his parents passed away, Tanguo Gong did not take food or drink for ten days;
overcome with grief, he vomited blood, fainting and then reviving. During the depths of winter, he did not wear padded clothing, and he maintained a vegetarian diet for the rest of his life.
Every time the anniversary of his death arrived, he was overcome with longing and grief; day and night he lamented in deep sorrow. Outside his gate stood two trees that grew evergreen even in winter.
Suddenly, a divine light would arise from the trees, and before long, the image of the Buddha along with the forms of his two attendant bodhisattvas appeared, their radiance brilliant and manifest.
Entering through the gate, they were seen by all members of Tan Gong’s household, both great and small, who together prostrated themselves for a long time.
It was then extinguished. Monastics and laypeople alike from near and far spread this account.
According to the *Biography of Prince Zhāomíng*: "The High Ancestor [Emperor Wu] extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma and personally delivered lectures upon it.

The Crown Prince likewise revered and believed in the Triple Gem and perused all the various scriptures. He subsequently established the Huìyì Hall within the palace specifically for the purpose of assembling for the Dharma."
He summoned eminent monks to engage in unceasing discourse. The Prince himself established the doctrine of the *dharmakāya* according to the Three Truths, all of which contained novel insights.
In the fourth month of the first year of the Putong era, heavenly nectar descended upon Huiyi Hall; everyone considered this to have been moved by his supreme virtue.

The Biography of Prince Wei, the Yuanxiang of Nanping. In his later years, Wei venerated and believed in Buddhist principles; he was particularly proficient in the study of the *Mysterious* (Xuanxue).

He authored the *Two Purports* (*Erzhiyi*), which presented a distinct and novel interpretation. He also composed treatises on such topics as nature and emotion (*xingqing*), the subtle and the spirit (*jishen*), among others.
Although the monks Sengchong and Zhou She, along with Yin Jun and Lu Chui, were all renowned for their refined understanding [of Buddhism], none could prevail over him.
The Biography of Prince Huai of Poyang, Zhonglie. Huai was naturally filial. When he was first stationed in Shu, his biological mother, Lady Fei, remained in the capital.
Later, while she was ill in the capital, Huai was unaware of it. One night, he suddenly dreamed that he had returned to attend to her illness.

Upon waking, he was filled with anxiety and distress, immediately abandoning both sleep and food. Shortly thereafter, news arrived from the capital stating that Lady Fei had already recovered. Later, he also [suffered] with an eye ailment...
He had been blind for a long time. There was a monk from the north named Huilong who possessed the art of treating eye ailments. Daohui invited him;

once he arrived, Daohui suddenly saw a holy monk in mid-air. When Huilong applied the acupuncture needle, his vision was suddenly restored and became clear. Everyone remarked that this was brought about by the power of his sincere devotion.
He was named Duanzhenzi [折/目]. A native of Shen in Lujiang, he once suffered from thirst and dysentery during his youth, which did not subside for many years.
Later, while presiding over a lecture at Shifo Temple in Wucheng, he fell asleep during the day and dreamed of a Daoist master.

His physical appearance was extraordinary. He gave him a handful of medicinal pellets, which he consumed in a dream; from that time on, he recovered. People of the era considered this to have been moved by his pure virtue.
Yin (styled Ziji) was the younger brother of Dian. He once traveled to Wu and resided at the West Temple on Mount Huqiu, where he lectured on the sutras and treatises.
Disciples followed him there once again. Among the local governors and magistrates who passed through the region, there were none who did not [pay their respects].

He arrived. [Daoyin] cited the eternal prohibition against killing. Once, when a forest officer was chasing a deer, the deer came running directly toward him; Daoyin prostrated himself and remained motionless.
Furthermore, there was a strange bird, red in color like a crane, which gathered at the lecture hall and became as tame and familiar as a domestic fowl.
Previously, at Kaishan Monastery, Master Zang had encountered Daoyin at Qinwang Hill. Later, upon returning to the capital, he passed away on Mount Zhong. On the day of his death, Daoyin...
At Banya Monastery, he saw a monk who handed him an incense box and a letter-case, saying, "Present this to Layman He. Having spoken, the monk vanished.
When He opened the case, it contained the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (The Treatise on Great Adornment), which had never before existed in the world.

Furthermore, within the monastery, a pillar of bright jewels was erected, which emitted light for seven days and seven nights. The Prefectural Governor, He Yuan, reported these matters to Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei.
The Crown Prince, admiring his virtue, dispatched the palace attendant He Sicheng to present a handwritten edict in praise of him.
He passed away in the third year of the Zhongdatong era at the age of eighty-six.
The Biography of Liu Huifei. Huifei, whose courtesy name was Wenxuan, was a native of Pengcheng. He once traveled to Mount Kuang and visited the retired scholar Zhang Xiaoxiu;
they took great pleasure in each other’s company and consequently resolved to spend their final years there. Thus, he declined official office and resided at Donglin Monastery.

Huifei was particularly well-versed in the Buddhist scriptures and skilled in the seal and clerical scripts. While on the mountain, he transcribed Buddhist sutras by hand, totaling more than two thousand scrolls.
He recited over a hundred scrolls of scriptures that he had regularly memorized. Day and night he practiced the Way with diligent and tireless devotion, such that those far and near admired him.
Commentators say that since the passing of Master Huiyuan, nearly two hundred years had elapsed before there was once again such flourishing excellence as that of the Zhang and Liu families.

Biography of Liu Xu. Liu Xu, courtesy name Yandu, was a native of Pingyuan. Xu was skilled in the discourse on the Ultimate (the Daoist teachings) and was particularly proficient in the Buddhist scriptures.

He once attended lectures at various temples on Mount Zhong with his paternal cousin Liu Xiao; subsequently, they jointly constructed a dwelling by the eastern stream of Songxi Temple, with the intention of spending the remainder of their lives there.
The Biography of Liu Xiao. Xiao’s courtesy name was Shiguang; he was a cousin of Liu Xu.

When he was young, he once sat alone in an empty room when an old man arrived at his door and said to him, "Your mental power is courageous and fierce, and you are capable of mastering the mysteries of life and death; however, you must not remain stagnant in one place for long.
Having said this, he snapped his fingers and departed. Once Xiao had grown up, he applied himself with focused devotion to the study of Buddhism. There was a practitioner named Shi Baohui...
As for "Zhi" (the Record), people of the time could not fathom it. When he encountered Xu at Xinghuang Temple, [Xu] started in alarm and said: "To dwell in seclusion and study the Way;
to attain Buddhahood through purity. He spoke these three things in this manner.
The Biography of Yu Xian. Yu Xian, courtesy name Yanbao, was a rustic man from Xin. In his later years, he became especially devoted to the Buddhist teachings.

He established a dharma hall within his residence, where he performed circumambulations and repentance rituals without ceasing throughout the six periods of the day. He recited the Lotus Sūtra once every day.
During the latter part of the night, he suddenly saw a Daoist practitioner who called himself Master Yuan. His appearance and demeanor were most extraordinary;

he addressed Sengxian as "Master Shangxing," handed him some incense, and departed. In the fourth year of the Zhongda Tong era, while dozing during the day, he suddenly woke up with a start and said, "Master Yuan has come again;
I cannot remain here much longer. His complexion remained unchanged, and he passed away as soon as he finished speaking. He was seventy-eight years old at the time.
The entire household heard a voice chanting from the air: "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Pure Land of Amitābha.
(From the *Biography of Zhang Xiaoxiu*). Zhang Xiaoxiu, courtesy name Wenyi, was a native of Wan in Nanyang. He had extensively studied various books and specialized in the Buddhist scriptures.
He passed away in the third year of the Putong era at the age of forty-two. At that time, everyone in the house smelled an extraordinary fragrance.
Qi. From the biography of Kong Xiuyuan. Xiuyuan’s eldest son, Yunchang, was a devout believer in Buddhist principles and observed the precepts of the sutras throughout his life.
He held official positions reaching those of Consultant to the Prince of Yueyang and Vice-Governor of Dongyangzhou.

Biography of Xie Ju. Ju was widely read and deeply versed in many fields from his youth; he was particularly proficient in the principles of the Yuan school as well as the doctrines of the Śākya (Buddhist) tradition.

While serving as the Governor of Jinling Commandery, he frequently engaged in alternating lectures on the sutras and śāstras with eminent monks. When the retired scholar He Yin heard of this, he traveled from Mount Huqiu to attend.
Its flourishing was such as this.

According to the biography of Ziyang (Feng Ziyang): in the final years of his life, Ziyang deeply believed in the Śākya clan [Buddhism] and observed its precepts. He spent his entire life eating only wheat and vegetables.
He passed away in the second year of the Zhongdatong era. Emperor Gaozu issued an imperial decree to compile the *Zhongseng zhuan* (Biographies of the Clergy) in twenty fascicles.
Biography of Tao Hongjing. Once, Hongjing dreamed that a Buddha bestowed upon him the prediction of Bodhi, naming him the Bodhisattva Śaktimat.
He then proceeded to the Aśoka Stūpa in Mao County and vowed to receive the five major precepts.

Later, when Emperor Taizong of the Southern Qi dynasty was in Nanxu Prefecture, he admired Hongjing’s pure character and summoned him to the Rear Hall. After engaging in discussion with him for several days, the Emperor departed, holding him in the highest esteem.
This is recorded in the *Duyizhi*. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty was an ardent devotee of the Buddha-dharma; however, his nature was characterized by much compassion and forbearance.

He issued an edict throughout the empire that contributions of silk, gauze, brocade, and fine fabrics must not depict the forms of birds or beasts, fearing that during the process of cutting and trimming them, living creatures might be harmed.
This is the underlying intent [of this work].

In the *Fófǎjīntángbiān* (Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Fortress), it is recorded that Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty entrusted his heart to the wondrous Dharma and extensively surveyed the original chapters.

He compiled the *Fǎjí jì* (Record of the Dharma Collection) in two hundred fascicles and the *Fǎbǎoliánbì* (Linked Jades of the Dharma Treasure) in over four hundred pieces. Furthermore, he constructed the Zijing and Baoen monasteries.
When Emperor Yuan was the Prince of Xiangdong, he donated his palace to establish Tiangong Monastery and invited Fachong to reside there to perform Buddhist services.
Upon ascending the throne at Jiangling, he changed the era name to Chengsheng. He once composed a work titled *Jinlouzi*.
From the *Fozu Tongji*: Chen Zhen was the elder brother of Zhiyi. He served as the Military Aide (*zhongbing canjun*) to the Prince of Jin’an of the Liang dynasty.
At the age of forty, the immortal Zhang Guo examined him and said, "Your death shall come within one year. The Master [Zhiyi] ordered Zhen to perform the Fangdeng Repentance.
Zhen saw a signboard at the gate of a heavenly palace that read: "The Hall of Chen Zhen; fifteen years hence, you shall be born here. Subsequently, Zhang Guo...

He saw a needle and asked in astonishment, "What medicine are you taking? He replied, "I am merely practicing repentance. The physician said, "If it were not for the power of the Way, how could you transcend death?
In the end, his life was extended by fifteen years before he passed away. The Great Master Zhiyi once composed the *Xiuzhengxiu Xiao Zhiguan* (Abridged Stop-and-Contemplate) for him;
he consulted and received its instructions, practicing them day and night without slackening.

From the *Book of Chen*, the biography of Jiang Zong. Zong once recounted his own life in brief, saying: "I have ascended through various high and honorable positions and served in full rank within the court.
I did not seek worldly profit, nor did I involve myself with those of power and fortune. I would often reflect upon my own conduct and look up to heaven, sighing deeply:

'Zhuang Qingzhi reached the rank of Chancellor, yet he left no trace worth recording; Zhao Yuanshu served as a provincial census official, yet his name shines brightly in the annals. While serving in the Chen dynasty..."

Since then, he has never encountered or engaged with a single thing, nor has he intervened in a single matter. Amidst the drifting dust of the world, those of common and worldly character have often harbored resentment and hatred toward him;
yet he pays no heed to honor or decline, favor or disgrace. During the Taijian era, power was usurped by a clique of petty men.

Deceitful and envious, he exercised authority and was repeatedly demoted and dismissed; alas, what can one do about destiny? When the Later Sovereign formerly resided at the Eastern Court, he took great interest in literature and the arts.
Having long been favored by his illustrious advancement, their bonds of grace and duty were profound. On the day he succeeded to the throne, the misplaced honor bestowed upon him was immense.

He presided over the capital and rectified the myriad affairs of state; there were no matters among the Eight Methods and Six Codes that he did not govern. Formerly, Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty [conferred honors] upon Xun... [text fragmentary].
The Duke once said: "The Chief Minister (Zǒngshǐ) of the Zhou dynasty is equivalent to the Chancellor (Shàngshūlìng) of today.

Moreover, if one's talent does not even equal half that of the ancients yet one occupies office like a mere figurehead or a parasite, it is as the Jin Grand Marshal (Tàiwěi) Lu Wàn said: 'To appoint me as one of the Three Ducal Ministers is to acknowledge that there is no one else in the world.'"

The carriage and the official cap are but transient things that come of their own accord; how could they be what one seeks in advance? Since my youth, I have turned my heart toward the Buddhist teachings.
At the age of twenty-something, I entered Mount Zhongshan and received the Bodhisattva precepts from Master Ze at Lingyao Temple.

In my later years, while serving in the Chen court, I formed a close friendship with the venerable Master Bu of Mount She, through which I deeply realized the truth of suffering and emptiness. I further refined my observance of the precepts, directing all my virtuous efforts toward the mind.
I have practiced compassion toward all beings and have known how to exert myself in self-discipline; yet, I am unable to live on simple vegetarian fare and remain stained by worldly toil.
For this, I carry a sense of shame throughout my life. This is my general self-narrative, which contemporaries call a "record of reality."
The Biography of Yao Cha: In his youth, Yao Cha once went to Master Shang of Mingqing Temple on Mount Zhong to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

When he entered government service under the Chen dynasty, he donated all his emoluments to the temple for its construction and posthumously erected a stele for the Master; the inscription was exceptionally forceful and elegant.

Later, while there, he happened to encounter a calligraphic work by Xiao Ziyun, the Libationer of the Academy of State Learning during the Liang dynasty, which contained a poem written for the meditation hall of that temple. Upon reading it...
Feeling deeply moved by this, he composed a poem in the *xiao* rhyme to express his sentiments; the lyrics were so poignant that both monastics and laypeople praised him all the more for it.
Sengcha wished to read through one entire Tripitaka collection, and having completed it, as he approached the end of his life, he experienced no pain or distress.
He simply sat facing west with right mindfulness, saying, "All things are empty and quiescent. Subsequently, his body became supple and his complexion remained as usual. Sengcha—
He was well-versed in the Buddhist scriptures (*abhidharma*). The temple towers and monastic writings he composed were particularly elegant and refined.
Wang Gu’s biography states that Gu was pure, detached, and free from desire; he was renowned for his filial piety during the mourning period. Furthermore, he held deep faith in the Buddha-dharma.

Upon encountering the mourning for his biological mother, he subsequently abstained from meat for the rest of his life. By night he practiced *dhyāna* (seated meditation), and by day he recited Buddhist sutras, while simultaneously cultivating [his spiritual attainments].
Although he was truly skilled in expounding the meaning of the treatises, he was not particularly adept in the original vernacular language.
Once, while on an embassy to Western Wei, during the course of a banquet, he requested that the slaughter of one sheep be suspended; the sheep then knelt and prostrated itself before Senggu.

Furthermore, at a banquet by Kunming Lake, the Wei people, knowing that Southerners were fond of fish, set out a vast array of nets; however, Senggu invoked the mantras of the Buddha-dharma, and consequently, not a single scale was caught.
Biography of Fu Zai. Fu Zai was a devoted believer in Buddhism. He studied the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) under Dharma Master Huilang of Xinghuang Temple and mastered its teachings completely.
At that time, there was the Dharma Master Daxin Gaofa, who authored the *Wuzheng lun* (Treatise on Non-contention) to refute [the *Sanlun*].

Fu Zai then composed the *Mingdao lun* (Treatise on Elucidating the Way) to resolve those difficulties. Its summary states: "The *Wuzheng lun* says: 'Recently, there have been those who propagate the *Sanlun*...'"
They mimic one another in their reproaches and denunciations, speaking at will of others' crimes and faults. They systematically disparage various masters and reject the teachings of all schools.

While discussing the Middle Way, they cling to biased views; while speaking of the state of non-attachment, they compete for individual victory. As they study the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika systems, they further treat them as enemies.
Once enmity is established, great strife breaks out. With such a mind, they accumulate karmic offenses. If these offenses do not cease, how could it be otherwise?
This further increases the accumulation of the great suffering of birth and death. [The interlocutor] replies: "The rise of the Three Treatises has been long.
Nāgārjuna initiated their source, eliminating the biased views of those within our own school; Āryadeva propagated their essential meaning, sweeping away the false attachments of non-Buddhists."

I desire that the Great Transformation flow without obstruction and that the Primordial Wind be propagated without decline. Its words are vast and its intent far-reaching; its Way is broad and its current deep.
This is truly the leaping and galloping of dragons and elephants, the soaring flight of the Kun and Peng.

How could those who are crippled, riding on wings that have not yet been shed, ever hope to rival them in this regard? Lately, the age has become decadent and thin, and there have been no men of expansive spirit. People have merely practiced the minor...

Through study, the ignorant mind is transformed; through gradual immersion, this becomes a custom, whereby one ultimately loses the true path. People compete only in their own speculative interpretations, each following their own constructions.

While the branches and leaves proliferate in vain, the fundamental source is daily obscured. One master’s explanation differs from another’s; they alter established doctrines and each establishes new intentions.
Even among fellow students, those who attain awakening differ from one another. Thus it continues in succession, becoming increasingly muddled and doubled over.

To employ them all at once without a definitive standard in one's mind, or to select and practice them while wondering which is correct—is this not like wounding the apertures of the primordial chaos (*hundun*) or damaging the sprouts of a noble tree?
Though others may say it is not a horse, you yourself hold the numinous serpent;
yet, with a cup that has no bottom, it is like painting a cake on the ground. In its failure to find the Way, is it not indeed fitting? Such is the learning of Mount She.

It is not like this. By maintaining the One and adhering to the fundamental, one avoids the fault of artificial fabrication. By condensing the text to express the meaning, one blocks off the tendency toward arbitrary judgment.
There is no prior discourse; the principle is not pre-constructed. Only upon encountering conditions does one respond; only after facing the adversary does one act.

Thus movements are纵横 (zōnghéng—transverse and vertical) and絡繹 (luòyì—uninterrupted), shifting between the sudden and the profound, sometimes encompassing all things without end, and sometimes dissolving into nothingness.
It is resplendent with patterns and texts, yet its traces and vestiges cannot be found. It is profound and immeasurable; it is encountered in immediate affairs and is not remote.
In all matters of response and dialogue, one should examine them in detail according to principle. What jealousy or deceit could there be to offend the various masters?

Furthermore, as for what these masters have taught, is it something that can be refuted, or is it something that cannot be refuted? If it can be refuted, then by refuting it, one brings about decline. If it cannot...
To criticize is not to fall short of the Dharma Master himself; why then do you alone shield and protect him so as to forbid such criticism?

Furthermore, there are Great and Small Vehicles within the teachings, all fully contained in the sacred scriptures. When the texts of the Mahāyāna point out and reject the "Small Way," how can one who now propagates the Great Dharma refrain from speaking of the intent of the Mahāyāna?
This, then, is a matter of praise and censure, a discourse of expansion and contraction, and of bestowal and withdrawal, proceeding from the study of the broad and the expansive.
Relying on scriptural discourse, how could one see the Buddha’s teaching and yet believe and comply with my own words while being in opposition to the Non-contention (araṇa)?

Is such an attitude consistent with a mind of equanimity? Furthermore, anger and affliction are the constant nature of ordinary people; those who have lost their decorum generally possess these traits.
How can you, despite having practiced the three trainings, remain unsatisfied and harbor resentment toward the Six Teachers, thereby concealing the wondrous Dharma of Nirvāṇa?
Never proclaim it. However, one hopes that once the mind of resentment has reached its limit, the awakening to profound tranquility will arise of its own accord.
Human countenances differ, and their minds likewise vary; some have words and intentions that contradict one another, while others have hearts and mouths in perfect accord.
How can one necessarily claim that others preach the Middle Way while their own minds remain biased? One’s own practice should be free from contention;

externally not conflicting with others and internally maintaining equanimity, how could enemies, strife, or litigation ever concern me? It is only those who accumulate sinful karma and engage in conflict who stand in fear.

As for the discourse on "Non-contention" (*araṇa-vibhāṣā*), the Great Master of Mount Shaodong’s method of guiding and transforming beings was not like this; rather, it was simply a matter of cultivation.
This is the practice of one who dwells in non-contention (*araṇā*). It is the virtue that guides others to awakening; it is the pure and unified style of the past.

Now that the turbid and competitive spirit has arisen, the perversity of slander flourishes here. My wish is to still contention in order to open the Way, and to relinquish victory so as to forget one's own merit.
Why must one refute and strike down other schools to provoke their anger? If one acts with a mind of the Middle Way, [one will not do so].

One who practices according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* is likewise able to remain without dispute. However, if one expounds the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* with a mind of partial attachment, dispute will inevitably arise.
Thus we know that dispute and non-dispute depend entirely upon a single factor. The response states: The Master of Sheshan was truly free from dispute.

Yet, what the Dharma Master has praised does not yet capture the full measure of his virtue. He dwelt in quiet seclusion within the deep valleys, remaining in a state of profound stillness and non-action.
In all matters of instruction and exhortation, there are none who are not of like mind; whether in leisurely speech or silence, nothing can create a rift between them.
Thus, although their intent is profound, their words are extremely concise. The current mode of expansive exposition is not suited to the present circumstances.

We dwell within the clusters of dwellings at the edge of the royal city, among guests who look about with every breath, and amidst scholars whose lips and tongues move restlessly as they brandish the sharp points of their pens and sharpen the feathers of their arguments.
With wings outspread, eyes clear, and courage bared, donning sturdy armor and grasping sharp weapons, they gallop forth with heterodox views and parade their divergent interpretations.
They watch for vulnerabilities and seek out flaws to engage in debate, weighing points of contention against one another. How could one remain silent and offer only submissive assent?
One must surely scrutinize similarities and differences and expose hidden defects; forgetting one's own person to propagate the Way, and defying worldly conventions to achieve penetration.
This teaching takes this very [dispute] to be a sickness; thus, one knows all the more that [the disputants] have not yet attained realization.

If the Great Master were in such a position, why would he necessarily remain silent, merely to be esteemed as a Dharma Master? Furthermore, the Dharma Master said: "My wish is to cease contention in order to open the Way."
To yield so as to forget one's own virtue—this matter of the Way and its Virtue does not reside solely in disputing or not disputing, nor merely in yielding or not yielding.
These words are simply what is esteemed in the human world; the Dharma Master admires them, yet he ultimately does not know how to "yield" in the sense of being surpassed.
If another’s Way is superior, then one’s own superiority is evident without the need for yielding. If another’s Way is inferior, [then one need not yield].
Thus, even if one offers a renunciation, it will be of no benefit. The words used to express such renunciation would then not be a mere empty formulation.

A mind that abides in the Middle Way can be realized anywhere; truly, what in the Three Treatises could possibly cause discord? One need only cease the interpretation of clinging to a stump and eliminate the intention of fixing a peg with glue;
in these matters, all are the Middle Way. Your letter suggests that the distinction between disputing and not disputing rests solely upon a single dharma—how is this so?
Is this merely to praise the "Non-contention" (araṇā) alone? Would that not be a contradiction? The *Araṇavibhāga-śāstra* states:

"Whether it be heterodoxy or orthodoxy, gain or loss, victory or defeat, right or wrong—all must arise from the mind. It does not mean that the Dharma taught possesses a fixed characteristic by which one may debate superiority or inferiority.
If one debates the right or wrong of differing doctrines, taking partial attachment as a fault, and speaks of neither right nor wrong to dissolve those gains and losses—[this is what is meant].
To consider this treatise superior and marvelous, such that other treatises cannot equal it, is also a fault. Why?

For when the mind of an ordinary person refutes something, how could there not be a mind directed toward the refuter? Thus, if the mind of victory or defeat is not forgotten, how can one not harbor a sense of superiority?
This is to boast of one's own attainment while discarding the faults of others; there is then acceptance and rejection, which gives rise to great contention over right and wrong.

This is indeed an increase of contention. He replied: "Speech is driven by the mind; the mind receives the designations of speech. It harmonizes the sense faculties with their objects and stirs the vital winds;

thus, speech is produced. All matters must originate from the mind. Truly, as the Tathāgata has said, it reaches the point that the real is created by the mind, while the false is employed through the mouth.
The mouth practices deception to respond to the mind; outwardly harmonious but inwardly treacherous, the words follow while the intent runs contrary, seeking only profit."

There are many such individuals—those who cultivate their reputations for fame, those who have entered the Path, and those who remain laypeople—for whom the Sage has thus provided detailed instructions and admonitions.
He has profoundly established preventive measures, describing the calamities and faults of the present and enumerating the misfortunes and harms of the future.

This text is as clearly manifest as the sun and moon. Yet there are still those who disregard their own bodies to violate stern prohibitions, treading upon boiling water and glowing coals, and willingly facing being ground to powder, all while acting with such determination that they look back at nothing else.
How could they take pleasure in the works of those who advocate non-contention and turn their heads to change their ways?
If those who propagate the Way and those who proclaim its transformation know in their hearts that it is superior, and speak of its superiority with their mouths, yet in their hearts...
Inferiority is in the mouth; it is also in the words. There is nothing hidden away, nor is there anything to be feared or avoided;
one simply acts with a straightforward mind. If another’s path is inferior, it is the teaching of the Sage. If one’s own virtue is superior, that too is the teaching of the Sage.
If I am superior, it is the Sage who is superior; if another is inferior, it is the Sage who is inferior. The superiority or inferiority of the Sage is indeed...
The faculties respond according to what is appropriate; whether here or there, what thickness or thinness could there be?

Even if one were to brandish a sword all day long or strike a wooden block through the night, glaring with bated breath to dispute gain and loss, or summoning one's spirit to seek victory or defeat—where would such things reside?
To speak of "having a mind" versus "being without a mind" is merely an attempt to differentiate the void.

For what reason do you not permit my discourse, thereby forcing me to withdraw in humility? This is like a *jiao* bird and a *peng* bird already soaring in the vast expanse, while the wary hunter still peers into the marshes in search of them.
Alas, O man! You ought to propagate this Way. Thus ends the *Wuzhenglun* (Treatise on Non-Contention). On Non-Contention:
The Way penetrates both the internal and the external. As for what you say regarding the necessity of debate, this is to use the derivative to rescue the fundamental;

it is to lose the fundamental while laboring over the derivative. Now, let me speak for you. Why is this? If we rely on external scriptures and trace back to the time before written records, [we find...]

In an age of ultimate purity, the mind is simple and unadorned; one practices the teaching of non-speaking. At such a time, people live out their lives until old age and death without ever interacting with one another, each attaining their own place.
What contention could there possibly be? Thus we know that non-contention from the very beginning is the true nature of things.
The response says: One must not hold to either contention or non-contention as exclusive; nor should one cling to the distinction between the fundamental and the derivative.
Furthermore, how can it be known? If they have never disputed in the past, how can one know that this is not the end? If they are disputing now, what proof is there that this was not the beginning?
Now, if one stands behind and looks forward, one is "behind"; if one stands in front and looks back, one is "ahead.
The matters of "before" and "after" are just like "this" and "that": when "that" calls "this" "that," and "this" calls "that" "that," the names "this" and "that" are merely relative designations.

As for where one dwells, by this it can be known that ten thousand matters are likewise understood. Regarding the fundamental and the derivative, the prior and the subsequent, the right and the wrong, and the good and the evil—how can these not be constantly maintained?
How can you presume upon your own cleverness to discard the eyes and ears of others? Indeed, bubbles arise and perish like foam.
The fire-wheel spins; one enters the pit of confinement and suffers. Bound by fetters, anxiety arises, and afflictions are provoked. What is the cause of this loss?
It is because one does not accord with the Way and gives rise to various views. For those who do accord with it, it is not so: there is neither non-action nor action.
Good and evil cannot coexist, yet one has never been apart from good and evil. Birth and death cannot reach them.
They likewise remain forever within the cycle of birth and death; therefore, one must attain permanent liberation and allow oneself to be free.

For this reason, the Sage, mindful that the shackles encircling them cannot be cast off and pitying how difficult it is to separate from the sticky glue, has taught with earnest diligence and provided every skillful means.

Those who aspire to cross over may seek a semblance of existence, yet while the horn of the qilin is difficult to perfect, the form of the elephant is easily lost; how can one not strive to approximate the truth?
Alas! On this long journey, you must exert yourself. During these brief moments, you should contemplate the good and evil within your own person;
do not speculate about other things, seeking to differentiate them by saying, "I am clever," "I have insight," "I am calculating," or "I am reflective.
To speak in such a manner is already superficial. Others are truly difficult to fathom; they may indeed be ordinary beings, or they may be as they truly are.
These sages condescend to accord with what is appropriate for the worldly customs of their time and perceive what must be seen regarding the retribution of karmic fruits.

How could they allow themselves to indulge their own inclinations and exhaust their personal natures to the point of giving rise to derision? They should simply empty themselves and roam through the world, moving up and down within the span of a flash of lightning or a drop of dew.
When the bright moon is in the sky, all the trees behold it; when the pure breeze is in the forest, all the pipes and flutes resound together.
How could I be one who opposes things? I do not enter the chamber of putrid fish, nor do I find pleasure in rotten rats;
how could I be one who conforms to things? Who can know me as we walk this path together—vast and magnificent! How could I again see contention as wrong and non-contention as right?
In this, those who contend contend for themselves, and those who do not contend do not contend for themselves; I take both and employ them.
It would be better for the Dharma Master to spare his labor and cease expending effort on pen and paper merely to address this "Disciple Free from Strife.

To exhaust one's lips and tongue while time slips away, engaging only with those who clarify the Way, is surely to engage in frivolous discourse regarding mere dregs. If you must examine what is true and what is false:
Let us briefly examine gain and loss. There is nothing superior to relying on the words of the sages and examining the principles of conduct and concealment.

By investigating from beginning to end and scrutinizing both the outward appearance and the inner substance, we shall ensure that empty rhetoric has no place and that deceptive paths naturally vanish.
Please wait for our future discussions to observe their subtlety.
Biography of Xu Ling. From his youth, Xu Ling revered and believed in the Buddhist teachings. He attained profound understanding of many sutras and śāstras.
When the Later Sovereign was still in the Eastern Palace, he commanded Xu Ling to lecture on the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Renowned monks gathered from afar like clouds;

at every lecture assembly, as they debated and deliberated with those in the four quarters, none could oppose him. His eyes had a blue tint, which people of the time regarded as a mark of intelligence and wisdom.
Xiao Ke was the third younger brother of [Xiao] Ling. He traveled east and resided in Jiayi Village in Qiantang.

There, he engaged in discussions on the Buddhist scriptures with various monks and eventually mastered the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises). Every day, he lectured on Buddhist sutras twice; in the evening, he lectured on the *Liji* (Book of Rites) and the *Zhuan* (Commentaries).

Among those who received his instruction, both monastics and laypeople, there were several hundred. During the Tianjia era, he was appointed as the Magistrate of Tan, but this was not to his liking. Shortly thereafter...

He resigned from his post once again. In the fourth year of the Taian era, he was summoned to serve as Director of the Secretariat, but he did not accept. He then subsisted on vegetarian food, observed the perpetual fast, and upheld the Bodhisattva precepts.
Day and night, he lectured upon and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Emperor Gaozong highly praised his integrity and conduct. Daokai passed away due to illness at the age of seventy-three.
At the time of his death, he sat upright while reciting the Buddha’s name; an extraordinary fragrance filled the room.
His vital energy was such that his neighbors were all struck with wonder and marvel.
According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs): Chen Yongyang Wang Bozhi, styled Ce-zhi, was the eighth son of Emperor Wen.

At the beginning of the Zhide era, he was appointed as the Regional Inspector of Dongyang. He requested the Great Master to go and preside over the lectures there, sending this invitation three times. The Master then...
The King, together with his son, Zhan, and their family members, collectively received the Bodhisattva precepts and observed the etiquette of disciples.

By day they listened to the lectures, and by night they practiced seated meditation. When the lecture series was about to conclude, he established a dharma-name for him called Jingzhi (Calm Wisdom) and composed a commentary, holding a great assembly.
He ordained people and cast images of Bodhisattvas. In his memorial, he wrote:

"I vow that in life after life, I shall always form bonds of virtuous friendship with the Dharma Master of Tiantai and the assembly of lecturers, both monastics and laypeople, and together turn toward the One Vehicle.

The Master said to his disciple Zhiyue, "I wish to urge the King to cultivate merit and avert calamity. Zhiyue replied, "The officials of the administration have not been long-standing associates; some may harbor feelings of favoritism and coldness."
He then desisted. Later, when the king went out on a hunt, he fell from his horse and was on the verge of death. The Master led the assembly in performing the Avalokiteśvara Repentance Rite;
consequently, the king regained consciousness slightly and sat leaning against a table. There he saw a Brahman monk holding an incense burner in his hand, who circumambulated the king once.
A fragrant aroma wafted about, and his agonizing distress was instantly relieved.
Shen Junli, whose courtesy name was Zhonglun, was a native of Wuxing. He was the son-in-law of Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty, being married to the Princess of Changgong of Kuaiji.

Holding the rank of Yitong, he received the Bodhisattva precepts alongside the Great Master. He composed a preface requesting the Master to reside at Waguan Temple and there expound the title of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The Emperor issued an edict to suspend court for one day and ordered his ministers to go and listen. At that time, Wang Gu, Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices; Kong Huan, Palace Attendant; Mao Xi, Minister of the Interior;
and Zhou Hongzheng, Vice President of the Secretariat, all donned the incense of the precepts and partook together in the wondrous Dharma.

They further requested to remain for an entire summer retreat to analyze and explain the fundamental meaning [of the teachings]. Monastics and laypeople gathered together, and many were brought to enlightenment. (Mao Xi’s courtesy name was Bofu.)

A native of Yangwu, he was fond of learning from his youth and was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts. During the reign of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty, he served as the Minister of the Five Armies.

At a Dharma assembly at Waguan Temple, he was granted the opportunity to join the audience. He earnestly sought the essentials of dhyāna and personally performed the rites of a disciple to receive the Six Subtle Gates and the Dharma-gate of the Forty-two Letters.
He studied these day and night, never neglecting his practice due to worldly affairs.

From the Biography of Cui Hao in the *Wei Shu*: Hao disparaged and defamed the Buddha-dharma, yet his wife, Lady Guo, revered and cherished the Buddhist scriptures, reading and reciting them from time to time.
Hao grew enraged, seized them, and burned them, casting the ashes into the latrine.

When Hao was arrested and imprisoned, he was placed inside a wooden cage and sent south of the city; dozens of guards were ordered to urinate upon him, and their wailing cries were heard far and wide.
On his journey, from the time he was subjected to execution and humiliation by the high officials, there has been no one like Hao. The world all considers this a manifestation of karmic retribution.
Originally, Hao, Yi, the Regional Inspector of Jizhou, and Mo, the Governor of Yingyang, were of nearly the same age;
Hao was the eldest, followed by Mo, and then Yi. Although the three traced their lineages back to different ancestors, Mo and Yi were closer relatives to Hao, who relied upon that fact.
His family had been among the high officials of the Wei and Jin dynasties, and they frequently insulted Sengmu’s chin.
Sengmu said to others, "Taojian may indeed deceive me, but how could he presume to slight my Zhou'er? Taojian was Hao’s childhood name, and Zhou'er was Yi’s childhood name.
Emperor Shizu heard of this, and thus he executed Hao; at that time, the two families were spared. Since Hao did not believe in the Buddhist Way, Sengmu [was deeply concerned].

He turned toward [the Buddha]. Every time [Dao’an] prostrated before an image even amidst dung and soil, Huihao laughed at him, saying, "To carry this skull and kneel in such an impure place—this is the way of a barbarian deity!"
In the twenty-third year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, which was the seventh year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of the Northern Wei,
Emperor Taiwu placed his trust in Cui Hao, who was wicked, sycophantic, and flattering, and held Kou Qianzhi in high esteem.
He was titled "Celestial Master" (Tiānshī). He cruelly harmed the Śākya clan, destroyed stupas, and abolished religious rites.
The ministers all said, "Kang Senghui moved Heaven with his auspicious omens, and the Great Emperor founded this temple. If you destroy it, we fear you will bring regret later.

Furthermore, within the inner palace, they dug into the earth and found a golden image; Hao then defiled it, whereupon his private parts became excruciatingly painful, and his cries were unbearable. The Great...
The diviner Shi Bu said, "Because you have offended a great deity, you must now offer extensive prayers at famous mountains and perform many sacrifices at shrines.

However, his pain became even more severe, and his inner anguish grew ever greater. A trusted palace attendant repeatedly offered this counsel: "Your Majesty’s suffering stems from offending the image of Śākyamuni.
If you pray to the Buddha, it may be possible to cease your pain. Seng Hao asked, "Is the Buddha a great deity? Let us try."
He sought [a remedy]. Upon a single request, he was healed. Overjoyed and having changed his mind, he went to welcome Dharma Master Kang Senghui with carriages and horses.

He requested instruction on ritual purification and repentance, received the five precepts, and came to hold him in profound reverence. Only then did he realize that Kou Qian had been secretly using heterodox and erroneous practices.
Consequently, they were subjected to severe punishment and banished to the four suburbs, where their bodies were buried with only their heads exposed;
even today, those who travel along the four main thoroughfares all use their mouths as latrines for as long as they live. As for the members of their sect, they were all executed by beheading.

It was not until the gengyin year that Emperor Taizu fell ill and finally attained awakening; furthermore, the barefoot Chan Master Tanshi came to enlighten him, leading him to feel shame and remorse.
He immediately executed Cui Hao. In the *renchen* year, Emperor Wudi passed away. His grandson Wen Cheng ascended the throne and immediately began the construction of Buddhist stupas (*bútú*).

After seven years, he restored the Three Jewels (*sānbǎo*). In the third year of the Heping era, the Imperial Preceptor (*zhāoyuán dūtǒng*) and Śramaṇa Fǎyào lamented that the former mausoleums had fallen into ruin and desired to restore them once more;
thus, he gathered the assembly of monks at the Stone Chamber Monastery (*shíshì sì*) on this terrace.

The translation of the scriptures was transmitted and circulated so that later generations of worthy disciples might maintain the Dharma-treasury, ensuring it does not fall into ruin for a thousand years.
Based on this instance of excavating the earth to obtain a statue, it is clearly evident that there was already proof of the existence of Buddhism during the Qin and Zhou dynasties.
From the *Wei Shu*, Biography of Gao Yun: When Yun was about ten years old, he escorted his grandfather’s funeral back to his native commandery.
He distributed the family property to his two younger brothers and became a śramaṇa, taking the name Fajing. Not long after, he disrobed.

The *Shilao zhi* (Biographies of Śākyamuni and Laozi) records that the *Sengtu* (Director of Śramaṇas) Tanyao, together with the Indian śramaṇa Candrakṣema and others, translated fourteen new scriptures.
Furthermore, śramaṇas such as Daojin, Sengchao, and Facun expounded various other [texts].
After Xianzu ascended the throne, his devotion to faith was even deeper. He perused various sutras and treatises and took a liking to the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
He frequently invited śramaṇas and scholars capable of discussing the ultimate principle (*yuan*) to debate the essentials of doctrine with him.

*Fǎbǎ Jīntáng Piān* (The Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark). Emperor Wénxì was personally fond of Buddhist studies; he frequently invited court officials and śramaṇas to discuss the fundamental principles of the Way.

Possessing a mind that longed for transcendence from the world, in the sixth month of the first year of the Yánxīng era, he issued an edict to abdicate the throne to his crown prince and moved his residence to Chóngguāng Palace, where he assumed the title of Shànghuáng (Retired Sovereign).
He established Lùyě Monastery in the Northern Garden and dwelt there with Zen monks, engaging in study and practice.
Essentials. From the *Wei Shu*, Biography of Wei Zan. Zan’s courtesy name was Zunyan. At the age of thirteen, he was appointed as a scholar at the Zhongshu (Central Secretariat).

He was intelligent and possessed clear discernment, earning the praise of the *Bo Shi* (Court Doctor) Li Biao. He was appointed as a *Mishu Zhongsan* (Secretariat Attendant) and subsequently promoted to *Shiyu Zhongsan* (Attendant Gentleman of the Palace Guard). Emperor Gaozu...
Whenever he engaged in discourse with eminent and virtuous śramaṇas, he recorded their exchanges in succession, leaving nothing omitted; he thus became quite well-known and appreciated.
According to the biography by Yang Qianzhi, Qianzhi’s father’s maternal uncle, Juqu Mengxun, had once occupied the territory of Liang, and [Qianzhi] was familiar with the state documents.
There were omissions and deficiencies [in his previous work]. Qianzhi then composed the *Shu liang shu* (Book on the Liang) in ten scrolls, which circulated in the world.

The state of Liang held both Buddhism and Daoism in high esteem, yet [Qianzhi] wrote treatises to disparage them, claiming that Buddhism was merely one of the Nine Schools of thought. Consequently, famous scholars of the time vied with one another to challenge him with Buddhist principles;
Qianzhi, however, responded to them using Buddhist doctrine itself, ultimately unable to be defeated.
The Biography of Feng Xi: Feng Xi was the elder brother of Empress Wenming.

He was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Master with the Right to Establish a Court, and Inspector of Luozhou, while retaining his former positions as Palace Attendant and Grand Preceptor. Although Luoyang had suffered through destruction and disorder, the ancient Three-Character Stone Classics remained intact.
Upon the succession of Feng Xi and Chang Bo-fu as Inspectors of the province, they proceeded to dismantle and divide [the stone tablets].
Consequently, [the state] fell into great decline. When Xi administered the government, he was unable to govern with benevolence and generosity;
instead, he placed his faith in the Buddha-dharma and used his private wealth to construct Buddhist stupas and monasteries across various prefectures and commanderies, totaling seventy-two sites.

He transcribed the entirety of the sixteen divisions of the scriptures and invited eminent and virtuous śramaṇas to stay, engaging them in daily discussions with tireless diligence. The expenses incurred were likewise beyond measure.
As for the construction of stupas and monasteries in various provinces, they were mostly built upon high mountains and prominent ridges, resulting in the injury and death of humans, cattle, and oxen.
A śramaṇa advised him to desist, but Daohui said, "Once it is completed, later generations will see only the Buddhist temple; who will know that it was built by killing humans, cattle, and oxen?"

The Biography of Prince Changshou of Chengyang. Changshou’s second son was Luan. At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Shizong, he was appointed General of the Pacification of the East (Pingdong Jiangjun) and Regional Inspector of Qingzhou.
Later, he was transferred to General of the Northern Defense (Anbei Jiangjun) and Regional Inspector of Dingzhou.

Luan cherished the Buddhist Way and practiced the five precepts; he abstained from wine and meat and maintained a perpetual fast for many years. He renovated and constructed Buddhist temples and exhorted the common people to join him.

The labor involved in such construction projects, along with the financial burdens and disturbances they caused to both the public and private sectors, became a significant source of distress for the people.
According to the *Biography of Pei Shuye*: Zhi, whose courtesy name was Wenyuan, was the son of Shuye’s elder brother, Shubo. From his youth, he was fond of learning;

he had thoroughly mastered the classics and histories and was particularly proficient in Buddhist scriptures. He excelled at discussing philosophical principles. At the time of his death, his spirit remained clear and his eyes were bright. In his final instructions to his sons...
After his younger brother’s life came to an end, his hair and beard were shorn and he was clothed in dharma robes;
he was buried with the rites of a śramaṇa on the northern slope of Mount Song at the age of fifty.
Biography of Li Tonggui. Tonggui was a native of Gaoyi in Zhaojun. He was the younger brother of Yi Shen, the Governor of Yangxia.

His physical stature was imposing, and his waist measured ten spans. He had mastered the various Confucian classics, reciting many of them from memory; he also studied the teachings of the Buddha and was skilled in medical arts.

At the age of twenty-two, he was selected as a *xiucai* (talented scholar) through the examination of essays (*shece*). He was subsequently appointed to the post of *fengchaoqing* (court attendant) and concurrently served as an assistant at the National University (*guozizi*).

He served as a Professor (Jiaoshou), was appointed Director of the Bureau of Rites (Dianyi) and Commentator (Zhu), and compiled the National History (Guoshi). He was subsequently promoted to Doctor of the National University (Guozibo Shi) and granted the military rank of General Who Subdues the Rebels (Zhenglu Jiangjun).
In the second year of the Yongxi era, Emperor Xing visited Pingdeng Temple; while the monks were lecturing on the Dharma, the Emperor issued an edict for [Tonggui] to engage them in debate.

His diction was refined and clear, and his exchanges were worthy of admiration; Emperor Wu praised him for this. During the Xinghe era, he concurrently served as a *Zhongzhi Sanqi Changshi* (Attendant Gentleman of the Palace) and was dispatched as an envoy to Xiao Yan.

Xiao Yan was deeply devoted to Buddhist studies; he subsequently assembled renowned monks at his two favored monasteries, Aijing and Tongtai, to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
He invited those of the same rank to attend the sessions, and Xiao Yan also sent several of his court officials, all of whom—
They observed and listened together, engaging in debate for a long time. Both monastics and laypeople alike considered it excellent.

When Lu Jingyu passed away, the Prince of Xianwu of the Qi dynasty summoned Tonggui to his residence to instruct the princes, treating him with great courtesy. Every morning, he would enter to provide instruction.
Only at dusk did he return home. Monastics and laypeople who requested instruction would follow him on his carriage as he traveled at night, and he would explain the teachings to them;
he did this during all four seasons without ever growing weary.
According to the *Youyang zazu*, when the Wei envoy Lu Cao arrived in Liang, the Prince of Liang sat in a small palanquin and ordered him to prostrate twice, then dispatched an official...
The Secretariat Drafter Yin Jiong conveyed the imperial decree to offer greetings of consolation. Upon arriving at the Heavy Clouds Palace (*Zhongyun Dian*), he was led up into the hall.
King Liang donned the robes of a Bodhisattva and faced north; the Crown Prince and those below him all likewise wore Bodhisattva robes, with attendants arrayed according to protocol.
Cao stood facing west in his proper order, while all the other officials were positioned in the western corridor facing east. A Daoist priest offered words of praise for the Buddha in three scrolls.
In the third fascicle of the *Zan* (Hymns), it is recorded that the Wei sovereign and the Wei prime minister, along with the men and women of both the northern and southern realms,
completed their prostrations before the Buddha at the Terrace and caused all their ministers to perform two prostrations as well.

When Li Xian and Cui Jie of the Wei dynasty arrived at Liang, they were welcomed at the gate by Wang Ke, the Director of Guests at Tongtai Temple, and the Secretariat Drafter He Jiyou, along with three monks who escorted them into the stupa.
Beside the Buddha statue stood a man holding a tablet and pen.
A monk said to Xian, "This is Shitou (Corpse-Head), who specializes in recording the transgressions of men. Xian replied, "He is truly the Donggu of the monastic community. They then entered further.
In the hall, there was a copper bowl before the Buddha with a lamp burning within it. Jie said, "This may be called the rising of the sun and moon while the torch-fire is not yet extinguished.
Regarding the ancestral vehicle of the first awakened ones: Yang Xuanzhi of the Northern Wei served as the Governor of Qicheng; he had long admired the Buddhist vehicle [and encountered] Bodhidharma.
Upon arriving in the Wei dynasty, he resided at Qiansheng Temple on Mount Yumen.

Xuanzhi asked him, "I, your disciple, have turned my heart toward the Triple Gem for many years, yet my wisdom remains clouded and obscured, and I am still lost regarding the True Principle. I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will reveal the essential tenets.
Bodhidharma spoke this verse: "Neither seeing evil do I give rise to aversion; Neither observing good do I strive to cultivate it. Nor..."
He abandoned wisdom to draw near to folly; he did not discard delusion to pursue enlightenment. He attained the Great Way beyond measure and penetrated the Buddha-mind through transcendence.
Not sharing the same orbit as ordinary beings or sages, he was loftily titled "Patriarch. Xuanzhi, his grief and joy mingling together, said:
"I only pray that you will dwell long in this world to transform and guide all sentient beings."
*Fozu Tongji*: In the first year of the Tianping era of Emperor Xiaojing, Han Xian, the Regional Inspector of Luozhou, had long been a non-believer in Buddhism.
At the Baima Monastery, there was a scripture chest from the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty that occasionally emitted a brilliant light; it was regarded by the world as a precious treasure.
Xian went to the monastery and hacked it open. Not long after, the local man Han Mulan incited a rebellion, and one rebel rose up from within a corpse.
He struck the virtuous man with a blade, severing his shinbone, and he died; people said this was the swift retribution for destroying a casket.
According to the *Beiqi Shu*, the biography of Lu Faho: Faho’s clothing, food, and dwelling were in every respect identical to those of an ascetic śramaṇa.
There was a young disciple who, in jest, severed the head of a snake and went to see Fǎhé. Fǎhé asked, "What was your intention in killing this snake? He then pointed to it to show him;
the disciple saw that the snake’s head was biting his trousers, yet it would not come off.

Fǎhé had him repent and perform meritorious deeds on behalf of the snake. Furthermore, there was another man who tested a blade on an ox; with a single stroke, the ox's head was severed. He came [to Fǎhé].
He went to see Faho, who said, "There is. A headless ox has appeared; the summons from your village is extremely urgent.
If you do not perform meritorious deeds on its behalf, the retribution will arrive within one month. The man did not believe him, but a few days later he died as predicted.
The Biography of Wang Sizong of Shangluo. Sizong’s son was Yuanhai. In the seventh year of the Jiande era of the Northern Zhou, he plotted treason at Ye City and was executed.
Yuanhai delighted in disorder and took pleasure in calamity; yet he feigned benevolence and compassion, abstaining from wine and meat.

During the final years of Tianbao under Emperor Wenxuan, [the Emperor] came to revere and believe in the internal Dharma (Buddhism), even to the point that no blood sacrifices were offered in the ancestral temple—all of which was the result of Yuanhai’s scheming.
When he served as the Right Vice Director of the Chancellery, he again advised the Later Ruler to prohibit slaughter and ban the sale of alcohol;
however, his fundamental intention was not upright, and thus it ultimately led to ruin and defeat.
According to the Biography of Du Bi: Bi was additionally appointed as Tongzhi Sanqichangshi and Zhongjun Jiangjun. He was dispatched on a mission to the imperial court. Wei...
The Emperor saw him in the Nine Dragons Hall and said, "I have recently been reading the *Zhuangzi* and find that its names and principles truly embody the Way (*Dao*).
Its attainment of the true source is identical to the 'Equalizing of Things' chapter. Having heard that you are a diligent student, I wish to ask you something:

in the scriptures, are Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) one and the same, or are they different? Bei replied, "Buddha-nature and Dharma-nature are simply one principle. The Emperor asked again:
"Since Buddha-nature is not the same as Dharma-nature, how can they be one? He replied, "Nature is omnipresent; therefore, I do not speak of them as two.
He asked again, "All who speak say that Dharma-nature is broad and Buddha-nature is narrow. Since their breadth and narrowness differ, how can they not be two?

Bi replied once more, "When it abides in the broad, it constitutes the broad; when it abides in the narrow, it constitutes the narrow. If one discusses the essence of nature itself, it is neither broad nor narrow."
"It is neither narrow. The Emperor asked, "Since you say it can become wide and become narrow, how can it be neither wide nor narrow? If it were definitively narrow, it could not become wide.
He replied, "Because it is neither wide nor narrow, it is able to become wide and narrow. Although the results—width and narrowness—are different, that which produces them is eternally one.
The Emperor praised his words as excellent and led him into the library of the scriptures, bestowing upon him the *Dhāraṇī-śīla-sūtra* (Dichizhi).
A collection of scriptures consisting of one fascicle and weighing one hundred bundles of silk.
According to the biography of Cui Xian: Xian served as the Minister of Revenue (Du-zhi Shang-shu) and concurrently held the office of Vice President (Pu-xie).

During the period of diplomatic relations between the Wei and Liang courts, high-ranking officials from both sides all dispatched envoys to accompany the official missions for trade; Xian, however, sought only Buddhist scriptures. When Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty heard of this, he had them transcribed for him.
With banners, flowers, and precious parasols, they offered hymns of praise and escorted him to his lodging. However, he was fond of grandiloquent speech and frivolous jesting, lacking all restraint;

he even commissioned the śramaṇa Mingzang to compose the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) and affixed his own name to it, which was then circulated throughout the region south of the Yangtze River.

*The Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark*. Yan Zhitui, during the Wuping era, served as a Gentleman of the Palace Gate (*huangmen lang*) and rose to the rank of Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*guanglu daifu*).
His entire family abstained from meat, and he placed deep faith in Buddhism. His work, *The Family Instructions of the Yan Clan* (*Yan shi jia xun*), circulates in the world.

Its "Chapter on Turning the Heart [to the Buddha]" states: "Matters concerning immortals involve expenditures of gold and jade and are largely empty and extravagant. Even if one were to attain immortality..."

One will surely die and be unable to transcend the world; therefore, I do not urge you all to study this. The matters of the three periods of time in the Buddha’s teaching are true and have verifiable evidence.

My family has long since turned its heart toward them, so do not treat them with negligence or contempt. The subtle principles therein are fully contained within the sutras and śāstras; I shall not further elaborate upon them here.
I only fear that your resolve may still not be firm, and thus I have briefly offered this earnest exhortation once more. As for the precepts:
Shaxun said: "The Confucian gentleman sees its life and cannot bear to see it die; he hears its cry and cannot bear to eat its flesh.
Gao Chai and Zeng Xi were unaware of the Inner Teaching (Buddhism), yet both were able to refrain from killing.

These are all instances of the natural application of the mind of the benevolent person. Among all classes of living beings, there are none that do not cherish their lives. One must strive to practice the abstention from killing."
To begin with, the four elements and five aggregates analyze the existence of form; the six vessels and three vehicles transport all living beings.
The myriad practices are all empty, and the thousand gates lead to goodness. This eloquence and wisdom is not merely the breadth of the Seven Classics or the hundred schools of thought;
it is clear that it is beyond the reach of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Laozi, or Zhuangzi. The inner and outer teachings are fundamentally one body, gradually...

These are extremely different; their depths and shallows do not coincide. At the initial gateway of the Inner Canon (Buddhism), five kinds of prohibitions are established, which correspond to the Five Constant Virtues of the Outer Canon (Confucianism):

the prohibition against killing for the benevolent, the prohibition against stealing for the righteous, the prohibition against sexual misconduct for the ritualistic, the prohibition against intoxicants for the wise, and the prohibition against falsehood for the faithful.
To turn toward Zhou and Kong while turning one’s back on Śākyamuni is to abandon the source for the branch.
How deluded they are!
According to the *Biography of Xue Shan* in the *Book of Zhou*: Shan’s younger brother, Shen, was selected to attend to Emperor Taizu while he studied.

Taizu, who was naturally fond of discourse, gathered one hundred eminent monks with profound knowledge of the fundamental principles (*yuanzong*) within his palace to lecture there, and further commanded Shen [to join them].

These twelve individuals, including himself, concurrently studied Buddhist doctrine so that they were proficient in both internal (Buddhist) and external (Confucian) teachings. Consequently, throughout the four quarters, people vied with one another to study the Mahāyāna.
According to the biography of Lu Guang:
Guang served as the Chief Secretary of the Prefectural Headquarters of Shanzhou. By nature he revered the Buddha-way, possessing the utmost sincerity, faith, and reverence.
Once, he accompanied Taizu on a hunt at Tantai Mountain. At that time, the winter hunt had already surrounded the area.

Taizu pointed toward the mountain from afar and asked the assembled officials, "Do you all see anything? They all replied, "We see nothing. Daoguang alone said, "I see a śramaṇa. Taizu said, "That is it.
He immediately broke off the hunt and returned, ordering Daoguang to stand at the spot where the śramaṇa had been.

He constructed a stupa; when he excavated the foundation to a depth of one zhang, he discovered a ceramic bowl and a mendicant’s staff, one of each. The Grand Ancestor (Taizu) praised this in admiration and consequently established a monastery there.

According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the first year of the Jiande era, there was a man named Li Lian in Chang’an whose spiritual anomalies were unfathomable. Every...

According to the *Qiyanyan lu*, when Lu Sidao was sent as an envoy to Chen by the Sui court, the Ruler of Chen used the name of Avalokiteśvara to mock him.
He asked, "What merchant is this, carrying such precious treasures? Thinking of the Way, [the monk] immediately replied using the words of Avalokiteśvara:
"May you not encounter an evil wind that drifts you away and causes you to fall into the land of the rākṣasa demons. The ruler was deeply ashamed.

Once, there was a guest sitting with him who did not believe in the Buddhist doctrine of karmic retribution, claiming that no such thing was heard of in the non-Buddhist classics. Shiqian explained to him, saying: "The accumulation of good brings forth blessings;

the accumulation of evil brings forth calamity. That noble families await their enfeoffment and those who sweep their graves look forward to the arrival of funeral processions—is this not the response of fortune and misfortune?"
