The Biography of Xinyanzhi. Yanzhi was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Luozhou; both his predecessor and successor administrations were marked by benevolent governance.
Furthermore, Yanzhi held deep faith in Buddhism and established two stupas within the city, each consisting of fifteen stories.

From the *Fofa Jintang Bian* (Compilation on the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark): Yang Su, styled Chudao, was a preeminent figure of his time for his extraordinary strategies and sublime compositions.
He held successive offices, reaching the rank of Shangzhuguo and being enfeoffed as Duke of Yue. He revered the Buddha-dharma and constructed Guangming Temple;
he also built Si-jue Temple at Mount Hua. Once, while Yang Su was practicing the Way, he observed a painted image on the wall and asked a Daoist priest, "What is this?"

[This is] a painting. Daoshu said: "The *Laozi huahu chengfo tu* (Painting of Laozi Converting the Barbarians to Buddhahood). Soso said: "I have heard that Laozi converted the barbarians. However, the barbarians did not accept [the teaching of] Laozi;
it was only when he transformed his body into a Buddha that the barbarians finally accepted him. Thus, it is the Buddha who was able to convert the barbarians."
The Way cannot transform others; why then speak of Laozi transforming the Hu? For what purpose would Laozi transform the Hu into Buddhists?
Why not transform them into followers of the Way? The Daoist masters were unable to respond. Pei Ji, courtesy name Yuanzhen, was a native of Sangquan in Puzhou.
During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he served as the Vice Director of the Jinyang Palace. When the High Ancestor ascended the throne, he said to Ji: "Send..."
"I have come here as a public servant. I pay my respects to the Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs.

One day, the High Ancestor asked his ministers, "Fu Yi constantly says that Buddhism is useless. What do you think? Jing replied, "In the past, when Your Majesty first raised the standard of righteousness, your will was set upon the Triple Gem.
You declared that upon ascending the throne, you would vow to open the Primordial Gate. Now that the six realms have returned to benevolence and the empire is prosperous..."
To rule the four seas yet wish to adopt the words of Yi—does this not diminish past virtue and manifest present faults?
In the *Tang Shu*, the biography of Xiao Yu states: Yu was fond of the Buddhist dharma and once requested permission to leave his family to become a śramaṇa. The Emperor granted his request;

however, Yu subsequently submitted a memorial stating that he was unable to do so, and due to foot ailments, he failed to attend court audiences. The Emperor said: "Could it be that Yu simply does not wish to?"

Regarding his misconduct, an imperial edict was issued stripping him of his rank and demoting him to the post of Prefect of Shangzhou. Not long after, his fief was restored and he was granted the title of Teci (Special Advancement).

[This concludes] the *Fofa Jintang Bian* (Compilation on the Buddhist Dharma as a Bulwark). Yu Shinan was a native of Yuyao, Yuezhou. In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, Shinan presented [this work].

The Commentary states: When this disciple was young, I suddenly encountered a grave illness. At that time, I resolved my mind that upon the day of recovery, I would provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand people.

Now, I respectfully offer vegetarian food to a thousand monks within this sacred precinct. By the power of this vow, I pray that in birth after birth and throughout all lifetimes, I may always be free from sickness and affliction.
May this same wish extend to seven generations past and distant future, and to all those—enemies and kin alike—within the six realms of existence hereafter. In future lives...
Yu Shinan passed away. Emperor Taizong dreamed of him and consequently issued an edict, saying: "Shinan’s virtuous conduct was pure and complete, and his will was set upon loyalty and benefit.
That he has suddenly followed the transformation of all things is truly a cause for grief. Last night, in a dream, I suddenly beheld this man, who further presented me with candid words."

He was like an old friend from my own lifetime. You may go directly to his home and prepare a vegetarian feast for five hundred monks and commission one statue of the Buddha to provide merit for his posthumous welfare, thereby expressing my intention to honor our long-standing friendship.
From the *Youyang zazu*: At the beginning of the dynasty, the monk Xuanzang traveled to the Five Indias to retrieve the scriptures; the people of the Western Regions held him in high esteem.

Chengshi once heard the Japanese monk Vajrasamādhi say that he had visited the Zhongtian Temple, where there were many paintings of Xuanzang wearing hemp sandals and holding a spoon and chopsticks, riding upon a multicolored cloud—things that did not exist in the Western Regions. Whenever it was the day of the vegetarian feast, [the image] would invariably...
I prostrate before this.

From the *Biography of Su Gui* in the *Jiu Tang Shu*: When Su Gui served as the Prefect of Tongzhou, Empress Wu was casting Buddhist statues and erecting temples and pagodas, with no year passing without such labor being undertaken.
Su Gui considered these expenditures to be vast and wasteful; although they did not deplete the state treasury, they nonetheless caused the people’s resources to diminish day by day.

[The state’s resources] will be exhausted; when the common people lack sufficient means, with whom can the ruler hope to achieve sufficiency? Among the monks and nuns of the empire, the genuine and the spurious are mixed together.

I request that monasteries be consolidated and that the number of resident monks be fixed as a permanent quota, to be replenished whenever vacancies occur. The Emperor found these words well-reasoned.

From the Biography of Wei Yuanzhong: When Emperor Zhongzong was restored to the throne, Wei Yuanzhong assisted in the administration of government, yet his reputation and prestige declined significantly.
A man from Chen County named Yuan Chuke wrote a letter to advise him, saying: "Now that those who have received ordination are so numerous, those in monastic robes occupy half the roads.

They do not take the monastic discipline as their foundation, but instead focus solely on using precious treasures to curry favor with the gates of power; all such positions come with a fixed price. In the past, when offices were sold, the money went into the public treasury."
The Prefecture. Nowadays, those who sell ordination certificates (du) have the funds enter private households; thus, those who enter the Way become mere itinerant consumers.
Upon receiving this letter, Yuanzhong felt even more ashamed.

According to the biography of Zhang Hao: when Hao was appointed as Minister of the Secretariat (Zhongshu Shilang), concurrently serving as a Chief Counselor of the Palace (Tong Zhongshu Menxia Pingchang Shi), he [recommended/promoted] those within the inner court.

Several hundred Buddhist monks resided within the imperial palace, where their quarters were known as the "Inner Dharma Hall. Their chanting and recitations could be heard outside. Li Ao remonstrated, saying:

"The fortune of the Son of Heaven lies primarily in nourishing the people. To seek beauty through a single casket [of scriptures] while the transformation of customs remains unheard of—how can this trivial Buddhism bring about Great Peace?
I pray that Your Majesty shall take 'non-action' (wuwei) as your heart's intent, and not disturb your sagely deliberations with the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The Emperor agreed.
Du Xian zhuan:
Du Xian’s cousin, Du Hongjian, returned from Shu and hosted a meal for a thousand monks, believing it would bring him merit. Members of the scholarly elite followed his example.

When he became gravely ill, he ordered a monk to shave the hair on the crown of his head and left instructions that he be buried according to Buddhist rites, without erecting a mound or planting trees.

Biography of Liu Yuanzo. Yuanzo served as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Bianzhou and Songzhou. In Bianzhou there was the Xiangguosi Temple, where it was rumored that sweat was flowing from the Buddha’s body.

Yuanzo went there in person and bestowed vast amounts of gold and silk. Thereupon, the military officers, civil officials, and merchants rushed to contribute gold and coins, fearing they would be left behind.
After ten days, Yuanzo issued an order to stop the collection; when he tallied the receipts, the total amounted to tens of millions, which he subsequently used for relief.
The military arts were largely of this deceptive and strategic nature.
In the "Biographies of Artisans," there was a man named Shi Yeyang from Jizhou. In his youth, he was a Buddhist monk; upon arriving in Chang'an, he gained an audience through Princess Jiuxian.
The Emperor, marvelling at his eloquence at the hot springs, bestowed upon him a crown and sash and appointed him as a Four Gates Doctor (Sìmén Bōshī).
The Biography of Wang Wei. Both brothers were devoted to the Buddha; they abstained from pungent foods and wore no ornate garments.
They possessed a villa at Wǎngchuān, a place of extraordinary beauty, featuring Huázigāng, Qīhú, Zhúlǐguàn, Liùlàng, Zhūyúpàn, Xīnyíwǔ, and other sites.
There they would stroll with Páidi, composing and exchanging poems as a source of pleasure. After the death of his wife, he did not remarry and lived alone.
After thirty years had passed, his mother died. Yuanbiao converted his residence in Wangchuan into a temple and was finally buried to its west.
According to the biography of Yan Tingzhi, Tingzhi was devoted to Buddhism; he was on good terms with the monk Huiyi, and after Huiyi’s death, he wore mourning clothes to escort the funeral.
He then buried himself to the left of Huiyi’s stupa. The gentleman [Liu Zhiji] considered this to be partiality.

*Fofa jintang bian*. Zhang Yue, courtesy name Daoji (also styled Shuo zhi), was a native of Luoyang. During Empress Wu’s examination of men of talent and integrity (*xianliang fangzheng*), Zhang Yue ranked first in his responses to the questions.
He was subsequently appointed as Left Assistant in the Palace Library (*zuobuque*). During the Kaiyuan era, he served as Chief Secretary (*zhongshuling*).

He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yan and posthumously granted the title of Wenzheng (Literary Integrity). His prose was refined and powerful; he was particularly adept at explaining the Buddhist scriptures.

He authored a preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (*Bore xin jing xu*), which states in brief: "The myriad practices arise from the mind; the mind is the sovereign of man. The Three Vehicles converge into the One;
the One is the source of the Dharma. To know that the mind has nothing to be attained is true attainment. To see the One such that nothing is not penetrated is perfect penetration."
Furthermore, he composed the *Dharmadhātu-maṇḍala-dharmāgāra-stotra*, which says: "The Buddha is the nature of space; The Dharma is the subtle light;
Concentration and wisdom are inseparable— This is the Saṃgha, the harmonious assembly. The person is empty and the dharmas are also empty; Even these two emptinesses are further empty.
Abiding in the mind upon the jewels of the three emptinesses— This is called the place of the Three Refuges. If seeing does not stain, And knowing does not grasp at consciousness—this is..."
This is called the "True Vision" and is also called "Liberating Knowledge. The Buddha contemplates that all phenomena are free from arising and ceasing; they are all thus.
[The Emperor] sent ten *jin* of fragrant incense as a gift, entrusting it to Wu Pingyi to deliver to Caoxi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch. There was a poem which said:
"The Great Master has departed this world, But his Dharma-body remains. I pray you send this unimpeded incense, To reach the South Sea with my heart."
The *Jiu Tang Shu*, Biography of Pei Xiu: Xiu was devoted to the teachings of the Buddha. He habitually abstained from wine and meat, seeking out and investigating their doctrines;

he elaborated upon and compiled them into tens of thousands of words. He practiced Buddhist chanting as his source of pleasure. He was on intimate terms with He Gan, to whom he even gave the monastic name "Xiang.
His contemporaries mocked and disparaged him for this, yet his fondness for these matters did not diminish.
*Beimeng suoyan* (Tales from the North Dream): Prime Minister Pei Xiu of the Tang dynasty devoted himself to the Śākya teachings and was proficient in Chan and Vinaya.

He took Master Guifeng Zongmi as his teacher and attained the sudden enlightenment of Bodhidharma. Master Mi composed commentaries on the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* and the *Chanquan*, both of which were prefaces written by the Prime Minister.
He frequently wore coarse woolen robes and went to the quarters of singing girls to beg for alms with his bowl, saying of himself: "I do not act out of worldly sentiment."
As for those who were influenced by him, he was able to teach the Dharma to them. He frequently made a vow that in every lifetime he would become a king to propagate and protect the Buddha-Dharma.
Later, the King of Khotan gave birth to a son whose palm lines bore the two characters "Pei Xiu.
Hearing that there was such a person among the imperial court, he wished to welcome him to his kingdom; however, [Pei Xiu] did not consent, and thus the matter was halted.

The *Biography of Pei Kuan* in the *Jiu Tang Shu* states that during the Tianbao era, he was ranked foremost among those of venerable virtue. Yet, moved by the Buddha, he delighted in associating with śramaṇas;
he practiced and recited their scriptures, becoming increasingly devoted to them as he grew older.
From the *Youyang zazu*: At the end of the Kaiyuan era, Pei Kuan served as the Governor of Henan.

He placed deep faith in the teachings of Śākyamuni and took the Chan Master Pují as his teacher, visiting him day and night. One day, Kuan went to visit Jí, who said, "I am currently occupied with some minor affairs and have no leisure for a lengthy conversation;
please wait a moment while you rest. Kuan then held his breath and remained in an empty room, where he beheld Jí.

He purified the hall and sat upright, burning incense. Not long after he had sat down, he suddenly heard the sound of knocking at the door, with voices repeatedly calling out, "The Master and Master Yi-hang have arrived!
Yi-hang entered and approached Jì to pay his respects. Having completed his prostrations, he whispered into Jì’s ear;

his demeanor was exceedingly reverent. Jì merely said, "There is nothing that cannot be done. When the whispering ended, Yi-hang bowed again. After the bow, he spoke once more. This occurred three times. Jì—
Weiyun said, "This, this—there is nothing that cannot be. Having finished this single phrase, he descended the steps and entered the southern chamber, where he closed the door behind him.
After a moment of silence, he slowly summoned his disciples and said, "Send for Master Zhongxing; he has passed away.
His attendants ran quickly to look, and indeed, Zhongxing had passed away just as Weiyun had said. Later, Huikuan donned mourning garments and buried him, traveling the entire way on foot.
He escorted him out of the city. Once the Emperor Yuanzong had summoned Xingyuan for an audience, he asked, "What are you capable of?
He replied, "I am simply skilled at memorization. Thereupon, the Emperor ordered the eunuchs of the Yeting Palace to bring the registers of the palace women and showed them to him.

After perusing them completely, he set aside the original text; yet his memory was so precise and proficient that it was as if he had practiced it all before. After reading only a few scrolls, the Emperor could no longer [keep up with him].
When the Emperor woke and descended from his couch, he prostrated before him and addressed him as a "Sage.

He was the first to realize the core teachings of the school. In the third year of the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, the imperial envoy Yang Guangting visited the chamber of Chan Master Benjing and, after paying his respects, asked:
"I, your disciple, have long admired the Way; I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will briefly grant me some instruction. Benjing—
[The Emperor] said: "The great scholars of the Chan school throughout the empire have all assembled in the capital. It would be sufficient for Your Majesty to consult them upon your return to court.
This humble monk dwells by mountains and beside waters, having no concerns to occupy my mind. Guangting prostrated himself in tears. Jing said: "Cease your obeisance to this humble monk.

Does Your Majesty seek the Buddha, or do you seek the Way? [Guangting] replied: "Your disciple’s wisdom and understanding are clouded and dim; I do not yet know the difference between the Buddha and—"
"What is the meaning of the Way? Jing said, "If you wish to seek the Buddha, the mind itself is the Buddha. If you wish to realize the Way, no-mind is the Way.
[The questioner] asked, "In what way is the mind itself the Buddha? Jing replied, "The Buddha is realized through the mind; the mind is manifested by the Buddha."
"If one awakens to the state of no-mind, even the Buddha does not exist. Jing asked, "How is it that no-mind is the Way?
Jing said, "The Way is fundamentally no-mind; no-mind is called the Way. If one realizes no-mind, then no-mind is itself the Way. Guangting prostrated himself and received this teaching with faith.
*Fozu Tongji*: Li Hua, courtesy name Xiashu, was a native of Zanhuang in Zhaozhou. He passed the jinshi and Hongci examinations on multiple occasions.
In the eleventh year of the Tianbao era, he was appointed as Right Supplementary Counselor (*you buque*). During the rebellion of An Lushan, he retired to live in Jiangnan.

Li Xian petitioned for his inclusion in his own military administration, and Li Hua was subsequently promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel (*libu yuanwailang*). Suffering from wind-induced paralysis (*fengbi*), he resigned from office and lived as a guest in Shanyang, where he exhorted his son...
His younger brother was Nong. Content with a life of poverty and austerity, he devoted himself to Buddhism in his later years; however, his teachings did not achieve great renown.

As for his writings, they consisted only of funerary steles for the families of scholar-officials and commemorative inscriptions for prefectures and counties. Whenever someone brought gold and silk to request them, he would reluctantly comply.
He once received the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) from Jingxi and composed a summary of its main principles in one chapter. At the beginning of the Dali era, he passed away at home.

The Biography of the Old Man of the Eastern City. The old man’s surname was Jia and his given name was Chang. During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he served as the head of five hundred youths at the Chicken Farm (Jifang).
When An Lushan seized Luoyang and the Imperial Carriage fled to Chengdu, Chang changed his name and took refuge in a Buddhist monastery.

There, he swept the floors, struck the bells, and applied his strength to the service of the Buddha. Subsequently, when the Retired Sovereign returned to the Xingqing Palace, Suzong received the mandate of succession.
At another palace hall, Chang returned to his old village. His residence had been plundered by soldiers, and not a single object remained in the house.
Wearing only coarse cloth, he appeared haggard and withered; he would never again be permitted to enter the imperial gates. The next day, he again departed through the southern gate of Chang’an.

On the road, at Yaoguoli, he encountered his wife and children. Their complexions were dark with the color of starvation; the son carried firewood on his back, while the wife carried old rags. Chang gathered them together to weep and bid them farewell on the road, and then—
Changshi Xi studied the Buddhist teachings under Master Fuzhi at a monastery in Chang’an.
In the first year of the Dali era, following the Venerable Monk Yunping of Zisheng Monastery, he went to the Sea Pond in the Eastern Market and erected a stone pillar inscribed with dhāraṇīs.

He was able to record his own name and surname, and while reading the scriptures of the Śākya clan, he was also able to comprehend their profound meanings. He used the Way to its ultimate extent and, with a virtuous heart, transformed the people of the marketplace.
He constructed monastic quarters and Buddha halls, planted fine grasses and sweet-scented trees, and by day he would carry soil to mound around the roots and draw water to irrigate the bamboos;

by night, he stayed in his meditation chamber practicing *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. In the third year of the Jianzhong era, when the monk Yunping’s life came to an end, after the funeral rites were completed, he erected a reliquary stupa at the eastern side of Zhanguo Temple outside the East Gate of Chang’an.
He personally planted one hundred pine and cypress trees and constructed [the structure].
He built a small dwelling at the foot of the stupa, where he burned incense and swept the grounds morning and evening, serving his master as if he were still alive.

When Emperor Shunzong was in the position of Crown Prince, he donated three hundred thousand coins to establish Master Chang’s Hall of Portraits and a refectory, and further constructed an outer building.
He lived as a wandering ascetic, taking only what was necessary for his sustenance. Chang therefore consumed only one cup of gruel and one sheng of rice-water daily;
he slept on a grass mat and wore a padded garment. Beyond these requirements, he dedicated everything to the Buddha.

*Fozu tongji*: In the third year of the Xingyuan era of Emperor Dezong, Liang Su, a Hanlin Academician, studied the Tiantai teachings under Chan Master Jingxi and deeply grasped their essential points.
However, because the texts and meanings of the *Zhi guan* were so vast and extensive, those who read them found them time-consuming.
He then edited and finalized it into six fascicles, which have circulated in the world. Li Hua, the Director of the Ministry of Personnel, once studied *śamatha-vipaśyanā* under Jingxi;
Jingxi composed for him a single essay on the general meaning of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, which encompassed the entire great work as clearly as pointing at something in the palm of one’s hand.
At that time, the gentleman’s fellow students were Cui Gong, Attendant-at-the-Immortal-Gate (Sanqi Changshi), and Tian Dun, Palace Counselor (Yanji Dafu);
both had studied *zhiguan* under Jingxi. During the reign of Emperor Xianzong, when the śarīra first entered the inner palace, it emitted a brilliant light at night.
At the morning court audience, the assembled ministers all offered congratulations, saying, "This is moved by Your Majesty’s sagely virtue. Han Yu alone remained silent. The Emperor [questioned him].

The Emperor questioned Liu Yu. Yu replied, "I, a humble subject, have once seen Buddhist scriptures stating that the Buddha’s light does not possess characteristics such as blue, yellow, red, or white;
this is the light of dragon spirits providing protection. The Emperor asked, "What then is the Buddha’s light? Yu was unable to respond.
Pei Du, the Regional Inspector of Hedong, memorialized: "At Foguang Temple on Mount Wutai, auspicious clouds appeared, and the Great Being Mañjuśrī was seen riding [upon a lion]."
A lion appeared in the sky with ten thousand followers, and from above, a messenger was sent to provide offerings for ten thousand bodhisattvas.
On that same day, auspicious clouds were seen within the temple.

From the *Jiu Tang Shu*, the biography of Liu Hun: Hun lost his father at an early age. When he was only ten or so years old, a shaman told him, "Your physiognomy indicates a short life and shallow fortune;

by following the path of a Buddhist monk, you may prolong your life. His paternal uncles wished to follow this advice, but Hun said, "To abandon the teachings of the Sage for heterodox arts is not as good as dying quickly.
Thereupon, his studies became even more earnest.
The Biography of Han Yu. At that time there was Jia Dao, a disciple of Han’s school, a native of Fanyang. He had originally been a Buddhist monk named Wuben.
When he came to the Eastern Capital, the Magistrate of Luoyang prohibited monks from leaving their quarters after midday. Jia Dao composed a poem expressing his distress over this.
Yu took pity on him and taught him how to compose literary works; he subsequently abandoned his Buddhist life and went to take the jinshi examinations.

Regarding the biography of Li Hanzhi: Hanzhi was a native of Xiangcheng in Chenzhou. He had small fists and great agility; initially, he was a Buddhist monk who wandered through the markets begging for alms, yet he obtained nothing by the end of the day.
Eventually, he discarded his bowl and cast off his monastic robes to gather a band of followers, attacking and plundering the area below Mount Wutai.

Zhong Chuan’s biography states that whenever he led his troops into battle, he would invariably offer prayers at Buddhist shrines. He would stack rice cakes and pastries to form the shapes of rhinoceroses and elephants, reaching several *xun* in height.
According to the *Zhuanglou ji*, there was a woman who removed her crown [to show respect] because she served the Great Being Avalokiteśvara with great solemnity; she went to visit a *bhikṣuṇī*.

He went to encourage her to practice the Pure Land method, saying, "You should perform the visualization of Avalokiteśvara and contemplate his Dharma-body; it becomes increasingly vast and increasingly wondrous.
From then on, she constantly saw him in her dreams at night. However, he appeared very small, like a jade Buddha atop a woman's hairpin.
One day, her husband sent her a jade Avalokiteśvara that resembled the one seen in her dream. From that time forward, her devotion to his veneration grew even more earnest.

Yùquánzǐ Yáng Xīgǔ was by nature an ardent devotee of the Buddha-dharma. He would regularly have monks stay in his residence, where he arranged Buddhist ritual implements interspersed with banners and canopies;
this was what he called a *dōuchăng* (place of practice). Every morning at dawn, he would enter its interior and prostrate himself upon the ground.
He had a monk occupy the upper seat and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* three times. His nature was pure and clean;
feeling an internal urge as if he needed to defecate, he would inevitably strip off his clothes until nothing remained, and only then proceed with high boots.

The *Jiu Tang Shu*, Biography of Meng Jian: In his later years, Jian became exceptionally restless and impetuous. His devotion to Buddhism was excessive, earning him the derision of his contemporaries.
He frequently collaborated with Liu Bochu, Gui Deng, and Xiao Mian in translating Sanskrit texts.

The Biography of Liu Bochu: Bochu’s son, Kuanfu, was appointed as Left Supplementary Censor. Chen Hu annotated Buddhist scriptures and, through the mediation of a court monk, reported this to the throne.
Consequently, he was appointed as Prefect of Haozhou. Kuanfu submitted a formal indictment against him.

Emperor Jingzong became incensed and said to his ministers, "Hu obtained this prefecture through a monk; how can an official of remonstrance accept such a statement? Kuanfu replied, "The multitude indicted Hu; I alone..."

The subject has drafted this memorial. [The offenders] should be executed; however, considering the source from which these words originated, I fear it may bring disgrace upon the state. The Emperor found his words sagacious and released them. (From the *Biography of Li Deyu*):
During the reign of Emperor Jingzong, Li Deyu served as the Inspector of Zhexi. Following the Yuanhe era, the empire had prohibited the private ordination of monks.
Wang Zhixing of Xuzhou deceitfully claimed that it was the Emperor’s birthday and requested the construction of an altar to hold an ordination ceremony.

People [sought him] to provide for their merit. The imperial decree was granted, and he immediately became prominent. He recruited followers throughout the Jianghuai region; the people all rushed to join him.

Consequently, he plundered and gathered their wealth for his own use. Li Deyu impeached him, reporting that Zhixing had established a ritual altar in Sizhou and recruited those wishing to undergo tonsure, requiring each person to contribute two thousand coins.
Thus, no further investigations or interrogations were conducted, and everyone was universally ordained. From the Huai River to the east, every third male household member was shaved.
It was certain that every male would shave his head, intending to evade labor service and taxes; those who were ordained numbered beyond calculation.
Your servant observed that those crossing the river numbered several hundred per day, and among the commoners of Su, Chang, and Qi, ten out of nine or eight were surely doing so.

If prohibitions were not added, then by the time the month of childbirth arrived, sixty thousand able-bodied males would have been lost to the regions between the Yangtze and Huai Rivers—a change no small matter. An imperial edict was issued to prohibit this in Xuzhou.

*Youyang zazu*. Tradition holds that when the monk Daqin went to Mount Jing, whenever someone asked him a question, he would respond spontaneously, yet his answers always reached the ultimate depths of the fundamental principle.
Liu Zhongzhou Yan once requested a verse on the mind; Daqin had him hold the incense burner and listen, repeating this process two or three times.
It is said: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Yan said, "Even a child three feet tall knows this.
Qin said, "Even a child three feet tall knows this, yet a centenarian cannot put it into practice. To this day, this is regarded as a profound principle.
In Chenggu County of Xingyuan, there was a girl of the Wei family who could speak at the age of two and naturally recognized characters.
She was fond of reading Buddhist scriptures. By the age of five, she had read through every scripture available in the entire county.

At eight years old, one clear morning, she perfumed her clothes, applied fine makeup, and sat silently beneath a window. Her parents were astonished; after some time had passed and she had not emerged, they went to look for her and found that she had already cast off her clothes and vanished.
In the end, no one knew where she had gone. Xu Bei, a retired scholar from Jingzhou, obtained this account from a neighbor of the Wei family.
Zhang Hongying, *Continuation of the Youyang Zazhu*: Li Zhengji’s original name was Huaiyu. He was the nephew-in-law of Hou Xiyi.

While Hou governed Ziqing, he appointed Huaiyu as the Military Commissioner. Soon after, Huaiyu spread slanderous rumors; Hou became enraged and imprisoned him, intending to subject him to legal punishment.
With no one to whom he could appeal his grievance, Huaiyu, while in prison, piled stones to fashion an image of the Buddha.
He was silently awaiting a karmic retribution in the darkness. It was near the day of the winter solstice; longing for his fellow practitioners, he sighed and fell asleep.
He woke to hear a voice speaking above his head, saying, "Li Huaiyu, your time for wealth and honor has arrived. Startled awake, he looked around but saw no one.
As it was still dark outside, he found the matter deeply strange and fell back to sleep. Again, he heard a voice say, "Look at the wall; there is a blue bird there."
The son cried out. This was the moment when the time for wealth and honor arrived; upon awakening, he no longer saw anyone.

After a short while, at dawn, suddenly dozens of blue birds, like sparrows, flew and gathered on the wall. Immediately, the sounds of three armies shouting were heard as they drove out Xi-yi, broke the chains to seize Huai-yu, and installed Fu-zhi as the successor.

From the *Fozu Tongji*: On a fast-day in the first month of the third year of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong, eight thousand monastics and laypeople from Mingzhou made offerings at the Śāriputra Stūpa in Ayuwang Temple.
They were moved by the falling of celestial flowers, white as snow, which would melt upon touching their hands.
At nightfall, the stūpa emitted light of five colors, causing the great assembly to rejoice and leap for joy.
*Beimeng suoyan*: During the Tang dynasty, Cui Anqian, the Palace Attendant (Shizhong), was a devoted follower of Śākyamuni and rarely consumed meat or blood.
However, regarding matters of criminal justice, he always personally oversaw them. Even when monks committed crimes, he never allowed the law to be bent.

When interrogating prisoners before the hall of government, he invariably maintained a warm countenance and showed compassionate sympathy to fully ascertain their circumstances. For those facing the death penalty, he would first have them shown the written judgment.
He was granted wine and food, yet he remained committed to the Dharma. During his three years in Zhenshichuan, he subsisted almost entirely on vegetarian fare.
The various offices provided wheat flour and kudzu products, which were dyed to imitate the colors of pork shoulders, lamb shanks, minced meats, and roasted meats;

these were all so lifelike they were indistinguishable from the real. Contemporaries compared him to Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, as he frequently performed puppet plays in front of the hall at the residence of the Imperial Commissioner.
Marionettes! Soldiers and commoners crowded the residence to watch, with no prohibition at all; yet the inner harem intervened in state affairs, thereby defiling such magnificent virtue. What a pity!
In the *Táng guóshǐ bǔ*, it is recorded that Li Dān, while serving as the Prefect of Qiānzhōu, wrote in a letter to his sister:

"If Śākyamuni were born in the Middle Kingdom, he would establish a teaching like that of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius; if the Duke of Zhou and Confucius were born in the Western Regions, they would establish a teaching like that of Śākyamuni. If heaven does not exist, it is as it should be;

if it does exist, only the gentleman shall enter it. If hell does not exist, it is as it should be; if it does exist, only the petty man shall enter it. Those who heard this considered him to possess true insight.

The *Dongguan zouji* records: When the Emperor was hunting west of the city, he gradually entered the Wei River and saw some twenty elderly villagers performing a vegetarian feast at a village Buddhist temple.
The Emperor questioned them, and the elders replied: "We are commoners of Liquan County. Our county..."

He caused Lord Li to implement extraordinary governance. When his term of office had expired, the common people petitioned for him to remain, going to the provincial government to request that he not be replaced.
This was surely due to the power of the Buddha’s blessings. The Emperor remained silent as he returned to the palace. Later, while at his private screen, the Emperor inscribed Lord Li’s name upon it.

Although the Secretariat twice proposed him for the post of Magistrate of Liquan, the Emperor struck through both appointments. Over a year later, he [was appointed] as the Prefect of Huai Prefecture.
[Text missing]. Please appoint a person. The Imperial Brush stated: "Li Jun of Liquan County may be appointed as Prefect of Mozhou.
[The Emperor's] intent was unfathomable. Li Jun bowed in thanks for the imperial decree of encouragement, only then learning of the matter.
From the *Touhuang zalu* (Miscellaneous Records from Abandoned Regions): The people of the south generally do not believe in the teachings of Śākyamuni.

Although there are one or two Buddhist temples, the local officials compel men to become monks as a means of tax collection and enforcement. The land and wealth donated to these monasteries are often seized;

occasionally, there may be one or two monks who delight in keeping wives and eating meat, residing merely within their own households and unable to understand even the slightest matters of the Buddha’s dharma. The local people provide daughters to such monks and address them by that name.
They act as priests for the deceased. If someone falls ill, they fashion round coins out of paper and place them beside a Buddha image, or invite monks to provide a meal.
On the following day, they slaughter sheep and pigs to eat; this is called "the ritual of exorcism" (chuzhai).

From the *Qīngyìlù* (Record of Refinements of the Extraordinary): During the Yì dynasty, the Buddha-dharma was highly revered. Monastic buildings exceeded prescribed regulations. When the Buddha’s relics arrived, the Emperor initiated the construction of the "Inconceivable Hall" (*Bùsī Táng*) to enshrine them;
when the work was half-finished, the Emperor passed away.

According to the *Yunxian Zaji* (Miscellaneous Records of the Cloud Immortal): When Feng Shaoying questioned Longhua Houcan about Chan, the Master asked, "What is it like when the golden rooster embraces its egg?
Shaoying returned home and sat in silence for three years, yet he was unable to attain realization; eventually, he went mad and died.
(Tu Shu Ji Cheng) Section on Divine Anomalies, Sub-section on Buddhist Teachings, Records of Events, Volume I.
(Tu Shu Ji Cheng) Section on Divine Anomalies, Sub-section on Buddhist Teachings, Records of Events, Volume II.
*Wu Dai Shi* (History of the Five Dynasties), Biography of Shi Āng. Āng’s father was fond of learning; throughout his life, he took no pleasure in Buddhist teachings. After his father died, Āng...
Before the coffin, he recited the Book of Documents, saying: "This is what my ancestors wished to hear.
I forbid that your household defile my ancestors with Buddhist rites."
Biography of Empress Liu of Emperor Zhuangzong of Tang. After Zhuangzong extinguished the Liang dynasty, his ambitions became arrogant and indolent;

eunuchs and performers corrupted the administration, while the Empress took control within the palace. Because she had risen from humble origins and had bypassed the proper succession to ascend the throne, she attributed her position to the power of the Buddha.
Furthermore, she delighted in amassing wealth, dispatching people to engage in trade as merchants, even down to the marketplace, where she [supervised] firewood...
Vegetables and fruits were all claimed to have been sold by the Inner Palace. Of all tributes from the four quarters, two portions were invariably set aside:

one to be presented to the Son of Heaven, and one to enter the Inner Palace. Within the palace, wealth and goods accumulated like mountains; yet they were used solely to copy Buddhist scriptures and to provide offerings to monks and nuns.
Consequently, Zhuangzong himself became a devotee of Buddhism. A Hu monk arrived from Khotan, and Zhuangzong led the Emperor...
Later, the Emperor and his sons went out to welcome and pay homage to him. As the monk traveled to Mount Wutai, the Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to provide provisions for his journey;
wherever he went, the cities and towns were moved by his presence. Furthermore, there was a monk named Chenghui who claimed he could subdue dragons.

Once, when he passed through Zhenzhou to visit Wang Rong, Wang did not show him proper courtesy. Chenghui said in anger, "I have five hundred venomous dragons; I shall dispatch one dragon to lift up a slab of stone."
The people of Changshan were all like fish and turtles. The following year, the Hutuo River flooded greatly, destroying the pass of Zhenzhou.
The city dwellers all regarded Chenghui as a deity; Zhuangzong and the Empress led their sons and consorts to prostrate before her, yet Chenghui sat calmly and did not rise.
Consequently, among the officials, whether noble or humble, all bowed to her, alone Gao Shi (Gao Chongtao) refusing to bow. At that time...

The Empress Dowager and the Empress maintained close relations with the regional military governors (*fanzhen*). The Empress Dowager issued "Edicts" (*gao*), while the Empress issued "Imperial Decrees" (*jiaoming*);
messengers from both palaces traveled back and forth along the roads. Wen Tao, the Regional Inspector of Xu Prefecture, was devoted to the Buddha;
consequently, he converted his private residence into a Buddhist temple to offer prayers for the Empress’s merit.
The Biography of Yin-sun of Ma. Having studied the prose style of Han Yu, Yin-sun frequently disparaged the teachings of the Buddhists.

Upon his retirement from office, he instead turned to the study of Buddhism and compiled the *Faxi ji* (Collection on the Joy of Dharma) and the *Foguo ji* (Record of the Buddhist Kingdoms), both of which circulated in the world.

His contemporaries mocked him, saying: "His devotion to Emperor Qingtai was not thorough, so now he comes to be devoted to the Buddha. Qingtai was the reign title of the deposed emperor. There was a person who...
Xi Yinsun said to him, "You have always admired the character of Han Yu, yet you frequently recite the arguments of Fu Yi; now you have turned to flatter Buddhism.
Is it that the Buddha flatters you, or is it that you flatter the Buddha? Yinsun replied, "How could I know whether it is not the Buddha who flatters me?
At the time, people circulated this story as a joke.

*Beimeng suoyan* (Tales from the North Dream): Li Jinquan, the regional commander of Jingyuan, had served in succession through various provincial commands. In every location he held, he engaged in extortion and submitted horses out of season.
When the Emperor asked him how his governance was, [Li] replied, "I have not specialized in the matter of submitting horses.

Although the Emperor reluctantly accepted this, His Majesty’s mind was not pleased. Zhang Qianzhao was excessively greedy; during his tenure as the governor of Cangzhou, due to a severe drought and the resulting famine among the people, he... [issued an order].
He provided grain relief for them. When the Emperor heard of this, he praised him highly. Later, when the autumn harvest was gathered, he doubled the tax collection; the courtiers despised this.
Qian Zhao was fond of engaging in Chan riddles and parables, saying of himself: "I know that my mind and my mouth are at odds; I seek only profit.
I do so solely by feeding monks, hoping further for blessings and rewards. Critics considered him a fool for seeking profit from the Buddha.
His excesses were extreme. Later, he rebelled and fled to Shu, where he seized people’s property and amassed wealth without satiety; the people of Shu resented him.
Someone once asked a Chan monk while he was in Shu, "What is a śarīra? The monk replied, "Simply renting out your residence will yield you a śarīra.
Qinghe merely laughed with shame.

*Fǎbǎ Jīntáng Biān* (The Golden Bulwark of the Buddha-Dharma): First, Emperor Taizu personally witnessed Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty melting down the bronze statue of Mahākāla Bodhisattva at Zhēnzhōu to cast it into coinage. Taizu secretly sought out the Monk Māyī and asked, "Since antiquity, has there ever been an emperor who destroyed the Buddha? Māyī replied, "Why must you ask about ancient matters? You may take the Imperial House of Chái as a witness. Taizu said, "I have seen this with my own eyes. Māyī said, "The Buddhas of the ten directions have all passed away; how could they possibly protect you now? Taizu was deeply moved by these words. He subsequently issued an edict prohibiting the destruction of Buddhist images and scriptures. This is recorded in the *Jìngdé Chuándé Lù*. Furthermore, the *Lóngchān Luòshèn Fǎshī Zhì* states that when Emperor Shizong of the Zhou first ascended the throne, he issued an imperial decree to destroy Buddhist temples throughout the realm. At that time, the monk Fǎshèng of Lóngchān Temple in Zhēnzhōu presented a memorial, saying: "The Buddha-Dharma is the foundation of the state; the Three Jewels are the source of blessings. If one destroys the Dharma, one loses the Way; if one loses the Way, the state will perish. Your Majesty’s virtue is such that even the birds and beasts know of it; how much more so for the people! To destroy the Buddha-Dharma is to destroy the state. If the state perishes, what benefit is there in destroying the temples? The Emperor read the memorial and granted his request. Thus, the decree was rescinded, and the temples were restored. This is recorded in the *Fǎbǎ Jīntáng Biān*.
