Thus, the decree was rescinded, and the temples were restored. This is recorded in the *Fǎbǎ Jīntáng Biān*. It is also stated that when Emperor Shizong of the Zhou first ascended the throne, he issued an imperial decree to destroy Buddhist temples throughout the realm. At that time, the monk Fǎshèng of Lóngchān Temple in Zhēnzhōu presented a memorial, saying: "The Buddha-Dharma is the foundation of the state; the Three Jewels are the source of blessings. If one destroys the Dharma, one loses the Way; if one loses the Way, the state will perish. Your Majesty’s virtue is such that even the birds and beasts know of it; how much more so for the people! To destroy the Buddha-Dharma is to destroy the state. If the state perishes, what benefit is there in destroying the temples? The Emperor read the memorial and granted his request. Thus, the decree was rescinded, and the temples were restored. This is recorded in
[Ma Yi] verified this. Taizu said, "The Sovereign is divine and martial, wise and capable of employing men well. He plots for governance day and night, with a heart set on unifying [the realm].
He possesses the spirit of Tang Taizong; I do not know when the empire will be settled. Ma Yi replied, "When the Jiazi year arrives, there will be great stability.
Taizu then asked, "Regarding ancient emperors who destroyed the Buddha-dharma, how did they compare to the Great Zhou?"
Māyī said: "When Emperor Taowu of the Wei dynasty destroyed monasteries, burned scriptures and images, and executed śramaṇas, neither father nor son met their deaths naturally.

When Emperor Wu of the Zhou destroyed Buddhist temples, confiscated the property of monks, and returned them to the common people, less than five years later, he was suddenly stricken by a wind-disease;

at the age of thirty-six, during his northern campaign, he perished in his carriage, and his kingdom soon followed in extinction. So too did Emperor Wuzong of the Tang destroy the Buddhist temples throughout the realm."
He reigned for six years and died at the age of thirty-two. The sacred regalia was transmitted once more, yet the rebel Huang Chao and his bandits rose up simultaneously.
Taizu said, "The world has long been weary of war; the destruction of the Buddha-dharma is not a blessing for the state—what can be done?

Mabei replied, "A white vapor has already appeared as an omen. It will not exceed several months until the year Jiachen, when a sage emperor shall arise in great prosperity. With his rise, the Buddha-dharma shall flourish."
Relying upon this, the state shall also flourish, and its legacy shall endure for generations without end. I request that the Grand Marshal keep this in mind.
Upon ascending the throne, he repeatedly established Buddhist temples and ordained monks every year.
Regarding the historical account of the Five Kingdoms: the Xu clan was about to transfer the mandate to the Yang clan.

Claiming that the Yang clan wished to enter the Way (Daoism), they constructed a residence on Maoshan and moved Liangbo to dwell there. They presented the "White Edict" for the abdication of the throne.

The elder official Zhang Jiuge conferred upon him the honorary title: Emperor Shanggao Siyuan Chonggu Ranghuangdi. After Liangbo had crossed the river, he composed a poem, of which the opening lines read: "Smoke gathers over Chu..."

The mountain peaks grieve with a thousand points of mist; raindrops fall like ten thousand rows of tears upon the Wu River. Four brothers and three hundred mouths—how can they bear to sit upright and contemplate this deeply?
When the time came for the assassination, he was just then reciting Buddhist scriptures on the upper floor as the executioner hurried forward.
Pu took his incense burner and hurled it at him; shortly thereafter, he was killed.
When Wang Yanhan, the second son of Wanyizhen, passed away, Wang Yanjun succeeded to his position and usurped the imperial title, styling his state as Daming and changing the era name to Longqi.

On the day he ascended the throne, having donned the ceremonial robes and crown, he suddenly became dazed and could not recognize himself; only after a long time did he regain consciousness, whereupon he made a mental vow.
He provided three million meals for the monastic community and had three hundred Tripitaka collections transcribed. Shortly thereafter, things gradually settled.

Later, he recorded the text of the vows he had made at various temples in a commentary, clearly describing these matters therein. Those who heard of it laughed and said, "The Great Min has truly attained such a state as 'responding to Heaven and obeying its mandate.'"

The *Fofa jintang bian* (Compilation on the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark) records that Wang Yanyun was a long-time devotee of the Buddha-dharma; he ordained ten thousand monks, whereby the number of monks in Min became great.
He once invited Master Luoshan to ascend the hall and preach the Dharma. As the master took his seat and adjusted his robes, he looked around to his left and right.
He then descended from his seat. The King approached, took Luoshan by the hand, and said, "How is this assembly on Vulture Peak any different from today?
In the *Jiangnan Yalu*, it is recorded that Emperor Li Houzhu of the Southern Tang was a fervent believer in Buddhism.

There was a monk who, together with the Empress, donned the *saṃghāṭī* robe and the monastic cap, recited Buddhist scriptures, and performed prostrations until their foreheads were worn down with calluses. He personally served as a *śramaṇa*, shaving [the Emperor's] head as if he were a commoner.
Jianzi tested him; his cheeks showed slight signs of stiffness. He treated him again, and his hands were no longer clenched. He learned to perform the *mudrā* of Avalokiteśvara while walking.

When a monk committed an act of adultery, the authorities prepared a document for his return to lay life; later, the ruler ordered him to prostrate before the Buddha three hundred times, whereby he was exempted from punishment.
When the Imperial Army captured Chizhou, he ordered both monastics and secular soldiers to recite the name of Guanyin Who Relieves Suffering.
The Bodhisattva Qian Shu, of the Qian family lineage as recorded in the *Song Shi*, was a devout believer in Śākyamuni’s teachings. Throughout his life, he constructed several hundred monasteries;
upon returning to the imperial court, he further ordained his beloved son as a monk.
The *Fofa jintang bian* (Compilation on the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark) records that Qian Hongzuo, Prince Wenmu, was the son of Yuan Gan.

He succeeded to the title of King of Wuyue and was posthumously honored with the title Zhongxian. He once dispatched the monk Huigui to Shuanglin to open the stupa of the Great Being Fu, the Master of Good Wisdom.
Sixteen fragments of sacred bone were obtained, along with countless *śarīra* relics the color of purple gold.
He then escorted the sacred bones, together with a pure water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*), an incense burner, a door-knocker, and other items, to the An-guang Palace in Qiantang for offerings.
He established Longhua Temple and fashioned an image of the Bodhisattva within it using the sacred bones. [This was commissioned by] Qian Hongchu, the ninth son of Emperor Wenmu.

He succeeded to the title of King of Wuyue and was posthumously honored with the title Zhongyi. Having long admired King Aśoka, he constructed eighty-four thousand stupas, each containing a precious casket;
within these caskets were placed the "Seal of the Mind" (Yinxin) mantras. After ten years of labor, the work was completed and the stupas were distributed throughout his domain.
On Mount Zhitishan in Fuzhou, there was a Thousand-member Retinue of Tianguan Bodhisattva; the King bestowed upon them the seven treasures and cast a celestial crown for them.
He fashioned one thousand statues and further constructed monasteries. When Bian Hao was first born, his parents dreamed that Xie Lingyun entered their room;
thus, his childhood name was Kangle. He served the Southern Tang as a Commandant of the Capital (Duyuhou) and followed Cha Wenhui in the conquest of Jianzhou.
All those captured were spared by him; the people of Jianzhou called him "Bian the Buddha's Son. Later, when he conquered Tanzhou, in the marketplace...

He did not cease his public preaching; thus he was called "Borderland Bodhisattva. Subsequently, when he served as a military governor (Jiedushi), he established daily vegetarian offerings and extensively performed Buddhist rites.
The people of Tanzhou called him "Master Bian" (Bian Heshang).

The *New Record of the Three Chu* states: When Wu ordered Bian Hao to lead troops to rescue Chu, it was in fact an expedition of conquest. Previously, Wu had intended to launch a military campaign against Chu;
because Hao possessed many skills, they sent him to travel through Changsha disguised as a monk, carrying a pair of cymbals (*ghaṇṭā*) while begging for alms.
Before long, he died and departed. Thus, Wu appointed Hao as general, yet Hao lacked the talent of a commander.

Every time he led an army, he would carry a Buddha image with him, offering prayers to seek blessings. Consequently, the three armies lost their cohesion; when Wang Kui’s troops arrived, they ultimately fled under the cover of night.
When the Prince of Chu, Ma Xifan, died, his younger brother Xiguang ascended the throne. His half-brother Xine, from Ding...
The provincial governor raised troops in rebellion and intended to attack Changsha. When Xiguang heard of this, he ordered his general Ke Qiong to resist him;
however, Ke Qiong turned his weapons against him and surrendered. With no other course left, Xiguang—who had long been fond of the teachings of Śākyamuni—donned monastic robes.
He summoned monks to recite the Buddha’s name as an expiation; even as the city was falling, he did not cease. Such instances of his ignorance are all of this nature. Soon after, Xi’e strangled him.
When they were gathered together, [the people] laughed heartily.
Before the founding of the kingdom, a Western Regions barbarian monk arrived in Shu during the time of the First Sovereign of the pseudo-Shu. Shu...

People gazed upon him with reverence as if they were seeing Śākyamuni himself. At the Great Compassion Samādhi Academy (Daci Sanxueyuan), the Ruler of Shu again visited him and sat with him in the hall.
The men and women of the entire realm flocked to the academy, and he did not stop them. The women lined up in order to pay their respects. A performer from the city of Rājagṛha proclaimed aloud:
"O female disciple, pray diligently in your worship! May your face and features in a future life be exactly like those of the Master. Shu...
The Lord laughed heartily.
The *Liaoshi*, in the biography of Emperor Yizong, records that Taizu asked his attendants: "In governing the realm, one must serve Heaven and revere the spirits.
Among those who possess great merit, whom do I wish to enshrine and sacrifice to? Which should come first? They all replied that it should be the Buddha. Taizu said, "The Buddha is not..."

Regarding the teaching of China, [Emperor Wu] said, "Confucius was a Great Sage and is revered by all generations; he ought to be honored first. The Taizu was greatly pleased and immediately established a temple for Confucius.
The Biography of Maguo. Maguo’s name was erroneously written as Tede. During the reign of Emperor Lanzong, he entered the imperial presence in his capacity as a minor official.

The Emperor asked, "Do you serve the Buddha? He replied, "Your servant recites every morning the edicts of the Taizu and Taizong Emperors, as well as the bequeathed instructions of our late ancestors;
I have not had leisure to serve the Buddha. The Emperor was pleased.
From the *Song shi*, the biography of Wang Renhao: During the Zhou dynasty, Renhao served as the Military Governor (Jiedushi) of the Shan-nan East Circuit.

At the beginning of the Song, he was promoted to the title of Grand Preceptor (Jianjiao Taishi). By nature, Renhao was upright, prudent, and frugal; he held deep faith in Buddhism. He devoted much of his stipend and emoluments to making offerings to the Buddha and providing meals for monks.
Every morning, he would recite five fascicles of Buddhist scriptures, often continuing until the sun had long passed the meridian before finally going out to attend to his official duties.

Incident: Liu Qian rebuked Renhao, saying, "Your Honor holds the noble rank of a regional prince, yet you cannot take diligent care of the common people; why do you instead devote yourself so zealously to Buddhism?
Renhao composed his demeanor and offered a humble apology without a trace of resentment. At that time, he was praised as a man of integrity.

*Iron Encircling Mountains Miscellany*. When the Founder first received the Mandate of Heaven, after some time he privately calculated that the Buddhists were divine spirits who caused suffering to the world;
"Now I shall suppress them, otherwise I will abolish their teachings.
One morning at dawn, he went out in disguise and entered the Great Xiangguo Monastery. As it grew dark, he suddenly arrived at a small courtyard. Looking from beside the door, he saw [the abbot].
A certain shaven-headed monk was heavily intoxicated; he vomited filth upon the road on both sides and was uttering foul abuse that was unbearable to hear. Emperor Yizu felt a secret anger.
Just as he was passing by from the side, he suddenly did not notice that the drunken monk had grabbed him by the chest and abdomen, holding him fast and saying, "Do not harbor evil thoughts;
moreover, it is already night. I fear someone might harm you; you should return inside; you may go quickly. Emperor Yizu remained silent.

His heart moved; he placed his hands upon his forehead and prostrated himself. The shaven-headed man then left him and departed. Emperor Yizu returned to the inner palace and secretly summoned a small, loyal eunuch, commanding:
"Go to such-and-such a place and observe whether this shaven-headed man is there.

Furthermore, bring back the description of the things he has vomited. When they arrived, the man was already gone. The eunuch alone scraped together the vomit that lay scattered on the ground. Upon reaching...
The Emperor inspected them and found that they were all made of incense. Consequently, the teachings of the Śākya clan were not abolished.
According to the *Xinlu of the Three Chu*: Initially, Zhou Xingfeng regarded excessive sacrifices as a nuisance;

he demolished all temples within his jurisdiction that did not belong to those who had rendered meritorious service to the people in previous dynasties. At that time, men of discernment rejoiced, considering this a clear and decisive judgment.

By the following year, he had become a fervent believer in the teachings of Śākyamuni. Every year, he established four great assemblies for vegetarian feasts (*kaṭhina*), which exhausted the state treasury;

furthermore, he continued to ordain monks and construct temples without ceasing at any location. On his leisure time, he would summon a multitude of monks to lecture and chant within the prefectural seat, personally holding an incense burner and burning fragrant smoke as he listened.
Indeed, among those clad in black robes, even children of only three feet in height all scrambled forward [to attend].

The Prince prostrated himself on the ground before him; even Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, though deeply devoted to Buddhism, had not surpassed him in this regard. Thus, the gentleman knew that his reign would not endure for long.
According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the third year of the Jianlong era of Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty, Zhou Xingfeng, the Prince of Chu, occupied Tanzhou. Indeed...

Although he engaged in acts of slaughter, he knew that he served the Buddha and ordained monks; he never ceased his practice of fasting and repentance. Whenever he saw a śramaṇa, he would immediately pay him homage and personally serve him food.
He said to those around him, "I have killed many people; were it not for the power of the Buddha, how could I resolve these karmic enmities?
In the fourth year of the Qiandé era, Shen Yilun, the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, served the Buddha and observed the perpetual fast. During the summer, he fell ill...

He sat there using his body as fodder for mosquitoes. When some remarked that it was suffering to have hungry mosquitoes swarm upon him and that he could not bear to brush them away, the ministers in office mostly rose to excuse themselves from their duties;
however, only Yi Lun remained, requesting permission to build a temple for his mother’s merit. The Emperor sighed in admiration and granted his request.
From the *Song Shi*, the biography of Kong Chenggong: Chenggong was granted the rank of Director of the Directorate of Works and retired from office.
He was a devoted follower of Buddhism and mostly subsisted on vegetarian food. Of the stipends he received, he spent more than half providing meals for monks.

He once exhorted the Emperor not to kill people and further requested that temples be constructed in areas of military conflict and that monks and nuns be ordained en masse. People remarked that his ideas were far-fetched and impractical.
Biography of Chen Sirang. Sirang served in succession as regional governors and military commanders; he was neither a failure nor a paragon of virtue. He was a fervent believer in Buddhism.
Wherever he went, he frequently prohibited slaughter and used his entire salary to feed the monastic community. People dubbed him "Chen the Buddha’s Son.
After his death, his family possessed no surplus wealth.
Biography of Li Chongju. Chongju was a devoted follower of Śākyamuni. He provided meals for as many as seven hundred thousand monks and constructed numerous statues and temples.

He studied Buddhist teachings and examined their precepts. Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty once enshrined Buddha’s tooth relic at the Great Xiangguo Monastery in the Eastern Capital. Emperor Taizong...
In praise of this, it was said: "Its layers of golden hue are lustrous; its single catty of jade-like radiance is cool. At that time, the court officials all praised it as excellent.
Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty frequently established topics for inquiry to test the Chan practitioners.
At that moment, Li Zunxu, the Prince Consort, was highly proficient in the study of the *Yuan* (the *Yuanjue jing*), and the Emperor bestowed upon him special favor and affection.
Record: During the Great Battle at the White Brook River during the reign of Emperor Taizong, the corpses of soldiers who perished in combat were piled across the fields.

The Emperor took pity on them and ordered their skulls to be collected and fashioned into rosaries, which he distributed to palace eunuchs to recite the Buddha’s name, hoping they might attain rebirth in a higher realm.
Furthermore, those skulls that were exceptionally large and deep were used to hold pure water for offerings to the Buddha; these were known as "Heavenly Skull Bowls" (Tianling Wan).
*Fozu Tongji*: In the fourth year of the Chunhua era, the Emperor visited the Kai bao Pagoda Cloister and asked a monk, "Who are you?

The monk replied, "I am the custodian of the pagoda. The Emperor said, "This is my pagoda; why do you act as its custodian? The monk was unable to respond. This occurred during the monk's audience with the Emperor.
The Emperor asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Woyun Hermitage on Mount Lu. The Emperor said, "In the deep recesses of Woyun, one does not face the court.
The monk was speechless. Once, the Emperor dreamed of a celestial being who said, "I request that Your Majesty give rise to the bodhicitta.
The following morning, he summoned those from the West Street to ask, "How is the bodhicitta to be given rise to? None of them could provide an answer.
*Fǎfǔ Jīntáng Biān*. Wáng Dàn, courtesy name Zǐmíng, was a native of Xīn in Dà míng. He served as Chancellor to Emperor Zhēnzōng and was posthumously honored with the title Wénzhèng.

In the second year of the Chúnhuà era, the monk Shěngcháng of Zhāoqìng Temple in Hángzhōu drew blood to transcribe the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and established a society for the cultivation of Pure Land practices.
Wáng Dàn was its leader. [Sū Yìjiǎn, Supervisor of State Affairs, No. 132.]
At that time, the officials and gentlemen all called themselves disciples of the Society for Pure Practice (*Jingxing She*). Among the participating bhikṣus were over a thousand people;
it was said that even the Lotus Society (*Lianshe*) on Mount Lu had never been as flourishing as this day. He passed away on the first day of the ninth month in the first year of the Tianxi era.
One day prior [to his passing], he instructed Yang Yi of the Hanlin Academy, saying: "I am deeply weary of this toilsome life.

I wish to become a monk in a future existence, to sit in meditation among the forest trees, and to take the contemplation of the mind as my study. After my death, please have a virtuous master come to shave my hair and beard and bestow the precepts upon me.
Let me wear the three robes for the cremation; do not place gold or jewels within the coffin. Yang Yi consulted with the orphans on behalf of the deceased, saying: "The Master..."

He was a Grand Duke (*sāngōng*). The ceremonial robes and funeral gifts of a Grand Duke include the *gǔn* robe; how could these be placed upon the body of a monk? One should simply place the three monastic robes (*sānyī*) within the coffin and not bury precious gems.
Regarding the discourse on death by the state elders: Wang Dan served in the Secretariat for twenty years; every day when he retired from court, he would go directly to his study tower.

He closed his door to seek solitude; even those family members with whom he shared the closest intimacy no longer had access to him. He frequently declined his office out of remorse for the locust plagues and droughts.

Shortly thereafter, he fell ill and ceased eating. Emperor Zhenzong commanded the Master of the Inner Kitchen to prepare minced meat, which the Emperor personally inscribed upon a vessel with his own calligraphy and bestowed upon him.
He consumed this three or four times daily. When his illness became critical at dawn, he gathered his family and said to them: "I have been unworthy for a long time..."
"It would be acceptable for me to sit upon the stage. Now I am about to die; I shall shave my head and don black robes to fulfill my lifelong ambition.
Before long, he passed away. His family members all wished to follow his words, but only his son-in-law, Su Qi, strenuously opposed and stopped them.
When Li Yunze was guarding Xiongzhou, the Xiongnu did not dare to graze southward, and the imperial court was free from anxiety regarding the north.
One day, he withdrew money from the government treasury in strings of cash and began collecting funds from the common people to construct a pagoda.

Immediately, slanderous rumors spread to the capital, and even the provincial inspectors repeatedly submitted memorials to have him dismissed. True Zong sealed all these documents and sent them to Yunze.
Nevertheless, those in the administration remained in a state of heated agitation. True Zong dispatched an imperial messenger with a secret edict to him. Yunze said to the messenger:
I am not one who has set my heart upon the teachings of Śākyamuni; I truly belong to a remote region and have merely constructed this watchtower.

At that time, the northern frontier was discussing the cessation of hostilities and the withdrawal of sentries; thus, I did not wish to make my preparations overtly visible, so that slander would not enter.

Upon completing his final tasks, the *Fozu Tongji* records that in the twelfth month of the fourth year of the Tianxi era, Yang Yi, the Hanlin Academician, passed away. Yang Yi had devoted himself to Chan meditation;
from the time he fell ill, he abstained from meat and pungent vegetables. On the day of his death, he composed a verse on the "Empty Gate" (Buddhism) to manifest his realization.
Zhi Shi remarked, "Those who know him well realize that he has attained the teachings of the Buddha.

In the *Huaman Lu*, it is recorded that when Ding Jingong was exiled to the south and passed through Yunshan Haihui Temple in Tanzhou, he provided offerings for the monks and brought so many monkeys that they filled the mountain valleys;
the trees were all broken down, and no further inquiry could be made into the matter.

From the *Guolao tanyuan*: When Ding Wei was exiled to Zhuya, he passed through Xiangtan on his way. At a Buddhist temple, he provided a meal for the monks and composed a prose piece to recount his own circumstances.
It states in brief: "Though I may have exhausted my skillful mind in mending the ceremonial robes of Zhongsan, I have failed to prepare the soup of Fu Yue."

It is difficult to satisfy the mouths of the masses. Once he arrived at his place of exile, he instructed the local people to fire tiles; first he constructed public buildings, and subsequently he established his own residence.
He built a small pavilion where he would go daily to read books and burn incense, remaining content and self-satisfied.

From the *Song Shi*, the biography of Chen Shu: Shu had long been disinclined toward Buddhism. He once petitioned for the abolition of the Translation Institute (Yijingyuan), his arguments being exceedingly vehement.
Zhenzong said, "The rise of the Three Teachings has occurred over a long period. Many predecessors have sought to destroy them, yet we may simply allow them to exist without engaging in debate."
Biography of Lü Dalin. When Fú Bì retired from office to his home, he devoted himself to the study of Buddhism.

Lü Dalin wrote to him, saying: "In antiquity, the Three Ducal Ministers had no specific administrative duties; only those possessed of virtue occupied these positions. Internally, they deliberated on the Way within the court."

Externally, the local educator presides over the community. When a great man of antiquity held such a post, he would surely have used this Way to awaken the people, perfecting himself in order to perfect others;
how could he have allowed it to fluctuate according to the rise or fall of his rank, or the waxing or waning of his physical strength?
Today, the Great Way remains unclarified and people flock toward heterodox teachings; failing to enter the school of Zhuangzi, they enter that of Śākyamuni, harboring doubts about the Sage.
Humanity has not yet reached perfection; they treat ritual and righteousness lightly, regarding them as unworthy of study. The human relations are obscured, and all things wither away.

This is a time for mature and great men to harbor compassion in their hearts, to take up the Way as their own responsibility, and to rouse the degenerate customs through their public efforts—this should be no difficult task.
As for shifting the essence and transforming the breath, striving to seek longevity, this is the business of those in mountain valleys.
To withdraw from the world and seek only to cultivate oneself is the preference of those who excel in solitude; how could it be what the world expects of you?
Bi declined the offer. [From] the Biography of Zhou Hang:

Hang was promoted to Shumishi Zhixueshi (Imperial Secretary of the Bureau of Military Affairs) and appointed as the Governor of Chengde Commandery. At that time, the local customs were such that people abandoned their kin to serve the Buddha.
Hang Yue reviewed and dismissed several thousand people and sent them back to their homes.

According to the biography of Cheng Hao: Hao’s father, Cheng Xiang, was transferred to serve as the Prefect of Hanzhou. Once, while hosting guests at a Buddhist monastery in Kaiyuan, just as the wine was being circulated, someone cried out that a Buddha-light had appeared.
The spectators scrambled over one another in a frenzy that could not be restrained. Xiang remained seated calmly and did not move for a long while.
...thus it was settled.

According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the first year of the Tiānshèng era of Emperor Rénzōng, the Emperor habitually wore a jade crown. Upon this crown, he had carved an image of Avalokiteśvara.
His attendants, finding the jade too heavy, requested that he replace it. The Emperor said: "The three dukes and the hundred officials, who all bow beneath me, are all [emanations of] Heaven..."
To bestow this upon a man of such distinguished virtue—how could I dare to presume to such honor? It is simply that, according to the distinction between sovereign and subject, it must be so.
By wearing this crown, I intend to cause the Great Being to return the courtesy.

*The Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark* (Fófǎ Jīntáng Piān). Lǐ Gòu, courtesy name Tàibó, was a native of Gànjiāng. In the second year of the Huángyòu era, Wén Fànzhèng submitted a memorial recommending him;
consequently, he was appointed to an official post at the Imperial Academy and subsequently served as a Lecturer (Shuōshū) at the National University.

He died shortly thereafter. He had previously authored the *Qiánshū*, in which he exerted great effort in refuting Buddhism. When the Venerable Sòng of Míngjiào brought the *Fùjiào Piān* to visit him, Lǐ Gòu was just then occupied with [his studies].
One day, while reading Buddhist scriptures, he sighed in regret and said, "Our own discussions have not yet reached the level of a single fascicle of the Heart Sūtra;
how can the Buddha-way be easily understood? A disciple of his named Huang Hanjie wrote a letter to challenge him on this point, to which [Wang] Guo replied.

In brief: the people’s desire for goodness is surely their innate nature. When the Confucian scholars of antiquity were employed by the world, they necessarily possessed means to instruct and guide them;
among the people’s ears, eyes, mouth, nose, mind, intellect, and hundred limbs, each had its proper governance—what leisure did they have to attend to heterodox paths?
But when the Confucian scholars of later times were employed by the world, they lacked such means to instruct and guide the people’s ears.
The eyes, mouth, nose, mind, and the hundred skeletal members—none of these have a presiding master. If one discards the Buddha, where else can one go?
Regarding the study of the Buddha and an examination of his teachings: Ou-yang Hsiung (Yung-tsu) frequently reviled and rejected the followers of the Buddha.

Later, while serving as Vice-Chancellor of State Affairs, he repeatedly suffered from dreams in which he arrived at a certain place where ten men wearing ceremonial caps sat in a circle. One of them said, "Vice-Chancellor, how did you come to be here?"
"You ought to return to your dwellings at once. After the Duke had walked several paces out the gate, he went back to question them, saying, "Are you not the Ten Kings spoken of by the Śākya clan?
They replied, "Indeed we are. From this, the Duke came to believe deeply in the Buddha-dharma.
Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty was deeply fond of Chan studies. Once, while reading the records of Touzi, he reached the point where a monk asked, "What is the white ox on the open ground?
Touzi replied by repeatedly shouting at him. Thereupon, the Emperor attained realization and composed fourteen verses on Buddhist scriptures.
The first chapter reads: "If you ask about the Master, True stillness merges with the vast void. Three heads and six arms— Mid-winter is truly spring."
Feng later presented it to Da’jue (Dajue). Liaolian then composed a matching verse.
Regarding the "Pure Conversations at Dao-shan," one day Chancellor Fu had a monk tonsured at his family temple.
Gongfu heard of this and laughed, saying, "Yanguo has ruined several men of talent by ordaining a single person. When asked why, he replied, "Whenever Yanguo..."
When he conversed with monks, he would often praise them excessively. Several people whom I personally witnessed became arrogant because of this and subsequently brought calamity upon themselves;
was this not their own undoing? Everyone laughed heartily, yet none failed to agree that his words were correct.
When Shao Kangjie and Fu Han-gong were in Luoyang, every day when the weather was clear, [Kangjie] would certainly...
They traveled together to a monastic residence. Whenever Lord Han passed by a Buddhist temple or a shrine to a deity, he would invariably bow his body in respectful salutation.
Kangjie laughed and said, "Is this not being sycophantic? Lord Han also laughed, and from then on, he no longer did so.
One day, while Lü Huisu was serving as Censor-in-Chief, it was reported that he was on leave at his private residence. The gentlemen there asked him, "For what reason are you on leave? at which time—
Liu Gongfu was seated there. Suddenly he spoke out loudly, "Today must surely be one of the ten days of abstinence.
This was because he was referring to Huishu’s fondness for Buddhism. Zhang Tianjue was also fond of Buddhism, yet he did not permit his sons to recite the sutras, saying:

"They have not read enough books and their spiritual source is not yet clear; as soon as they pick up a scripture, they immediately burn incense and prostrate themselves. They are incapable [of true understanding]."
Obtained. Someone asked Fan Jingren, "Why do you not believe in Buddhism?
Jingren replied, "Do you expect me to join my palms and prostrate myself before you only then consider it faith?"

One may discuss Yang Jie, whose courtesy name was Cigong. He applied his mind to the Buddhist teachings and once, when attending the imperial audience, the Shenkao (Emperor Shenzong) questioned him extensively regarding the general principles of Buddhism.
Yang did not provide a detailed response, saying instead, "Buddhism truly serves as an aid to our own [Confucian] teaching.

Upon his return, everyone censured him; some rebuked him, saying that a sagacious sovereign is difficult to encounter. Yet such was Cigong’s lifelong pursuit of learning—that he merely acquiesced with "yes, yes" (weiyi). How could this be?
Yang said, "The court’s intentions are upright and its discernment clear; I fear that [the Emperor] will act as a spiritual guide, so I dare not respond recklessly.
*Chunzhu Jiwen* records that when the Rectifier of Words Gong Yanhe returned from his place of exile to Weicheng County, he resided in a Chan monastery.

Every day he would carry his alms bowl to join the hall for meals. One leisure day, while passing through the administrative office (*kusō*), he saw a novice monk preparing noodles with broth and asked him about it.
The reason for this is that he provided the evening medicine and food for the monks in the temple courtyard; from then on, Gong no longer ate in the evening.
According to the *Chuijian lu*, Lord Wen did not favor Buddhism, asserting that its subtle teachings were not found outside the Confucian classics;
yet his family code states that in the tenth month, they would go to the monastery to provide vegetarian offerings for the monks, recite sutras, and offer prayers for their ancestors.
In the *Mian-shui Yan-tan Lu* (Anecdotes from the Mian Water), it is recorded that in recent times many scholar-officials have been cultivating Buddhist studies.
Sima Guang, the Duke Wen, was concerned by this and once composed six verses on the resolution of Chan to address it, which say: "Wrath is like a blazing fire; Sensual desire is like a sharp blade.
To be perpetually sorrowful throughout the day— This is called the Avīci Hell. Yan Hui found contentment in the humble lane; Mencius was at ease with what came naturally. Wealth and honor..."
Floating clouds: this is named the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Filial piety and fraternal duty penetrate the divine spirits; loyalty and trustworthiness prevail among the barbarians.

Accumulating goodness brings forth a hundred auspicious signs; this is called the law of cause and effect. It is the peaceful dwelling of the benevolent person and the straight path of the righteous person.

To practice it with sincerity and for a long time—this is called the indestructible body. Cultivating the Way and its Virtue within one’s own person, one’s merit and virtue extend to all things. Thus one becomes a worthy one.
O Great Sage, this is called the Buddha of the Bodhisattva. His words serve as teachers for a hundred generations; his conduct serves as the law for all under heaven.
Enduring for a long time, it cannot be obscured; this is called the Treasury of Radiance.
In the *Fozu Tongji*, Sima Guang once read the *Wen Zhongzi* and remarked that the Buddha was a sage.

He then said, "If this is indeed so, then the mind of the Buddha can be perceived. He subsequently composed six verses on Chan, the last of which reads: "His words serve as teachers for a hundred generations;
His conduct serves as a law for all under heaven. To be a worthy one and a great sage— This is what is called a Buddha or a Bodhisattva. [End of excerpt]
One day, while touring various temples in Luoyang, [Foguang] found the corridors not at all deserted. Suddenly, the sound of bells and drums was heard;
he went to the refectory and saw the śramaṇas sitting upright, silently beginning to take their first morsels with their spoons and chopsticks.

Foguang joyfully said to those around him, "I never imagined that the rites and music of the Three Dynasties would be found within these saffron robes. Du Yan, the Duke of Qi, frequently mocked Zhang Fangping for his devotion to Buddhism.
They found this strange. There was a physician named Mr. Zhu who moved between the two gentlemen. One day, Lord Qi summoned Mr. Zhu to examine his pulse.
The physician said to the messenger, "Go and inform the lord that I have not yet finished reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

When he arrived and was invited to sit, the lord said to him, "I considered you to be a man of refined and open character, but I did not expect you to become so dull-witted recently. The Sage had a subtle insight; there is no one who surpasses Confucius."
Meng asked, "What kind of discourse is this so-called *Śūraṅgama*? Sheng replied, "Since you have not read this sutra, how can you know it does not surpass Confucius and Mencus?
He then drew the scroll from his sleeve and presented it. Upon reading it, Lord Qi could not help but finish the entire volume; he was greatly amazed and said:
Seng'an Dao knew this, yet he did not inform me. I immediately ordered my carriage to go and see him.
Seng'an Dao said, "It is like losing an object and suddenly finding it; one should simply rejoice in its recovery, rather than regretting the lateness."
From the *Fofa Jintang Bian* (Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark). Wang Anshi asked Zhang Fangping: "A hundred years after the passing of Confucius, Mencius was born;
thereafter, no one appeared. Even if there were some, they were not pure scholars. Fangping replied: "How can you say there were no such people?"
"There are also those who surpass even Confucius and Mencius. The Duke asked, "Who are they?
Fangping replied, " Mazu I, Wuye of Fenyang, Xuefeng Cun, Yantou Huo, Danxia Ran, and Yunmen Yan. The Duke’s meaning remained unresolved, so Fangping said:
"The Confucian school has become insipid and can no longer retain its followers; they all turn toward the teachings of Śākyamuni. The Duke sighed in joyful admiration.
Later, he spoke of this to Zhang Shangying, who struck the table in appreciation and said, "How profound indeed is this argument!"
From the *Qingxiang zajì*: Minister of State Zhang Fangping was exceptionally proficient in the principles of human nature and destiny (*xingli*).

When someone asked him about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, Zhang replied with a verse: "Since beginningless time throughout ten thousand kalpas, The myriad dharmas have originally not been a single dharma.
I do not know the Patriarch’s intent in coming from the West; One night, the western wind sweeps away the yellow leaves."

*Suoyu Ji* (The Collection of Spittle and Jade). Zhang Shangying, styled Tianjue and nicknamed Wujin, once saw Buddhist scriptures neatly arranged and lamented that our Confucianists were not their equal.
At night he took up his brush; his wife, Lady Xiang, asked what he was composing. He replied, "I wish to write a *Wufo Lun* (Treatise on the Non-existence of Buddha).
Lady Xiang said, "If you say there is 'no' [Buddha], then why discuss it? Startled by her words, he desisted. Later, while reading the *Zangjing* (Tripitaka), he underwent a sudden transformation.
Wu then composed the *Fahulun* (Treatise on Protecting the Dharma).

According to the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the fourth year of the Qingli era, the Censor-in-Chief Ouyang Xiu was implicated by a denunciant and cast into the imperial prison for interrogation;
he was subsequently demoted to Chuzhou. The following year, as he was returning to Luling, his boat stopped at Jiujiang, whereupon he entrusted [the work]...
Xiu traveled to Mount Lu and entered the Yuantong Monastery of Donglin to pay his respects to Chan Master Zuyin. There, Xiu discussed the Way with him;

the Master had traversed the teachings of a hundred schools before finding his final resolution in the Buddha-dharma. Xiu was profoundly moved by his sincerity and submitted himself to him in heart, listening intently until he forgot all weariness.

When night fell, he could not stop himself; he silently nodded his head in agreement. Although he had habitually disparaged Buddhism, for this reason he withdrew his opposition and hesitated to leave.
After more than ten days, he could not bear to depart. Some have said that this is precisely analogous to Han Yu’s meeting with Dadian.

When Xiu first arrived at the Master’s quarters, the Master gestured for him to be seated and said, "You have traveled far to visit me; surely it is because the Way of the Sage of India accords with [your own]?"
Xinhu Xi responded with a haughty air, saying, "I have studied the Way of Confucius and Mencius and secretly admire Han Yu’s rejection of Buddhism and Daoism.
As for the Dharma of Western India, what is there to be gained from it? The Master looked sternly at him and interrogated him, saying:

Liu Zongyuan (Tui-zhi) sought to exclude Buddhism and Daoism, comparing himself to Mencius in his opposition to Yang Zhu and Mo Di. However, the Buddhas and the Great Sages are not comparable to Yang and Mo;
since even Liu Zongyuan should not have excluded them, how much less so those who today wish to emulate them? This was the statement of Wenzhongzi in the past.
"The Buddha was a sage, yet you have relegated him to the rank of a barbarian ghost. This is a statement of great arrogance. Xiu replied, "Scholars have abandoned the Middle Way teachings;
historians have not established a biography for him; and you, Master Tu, have ceased speaking of him altogether. Now, you [Master Zongmi] cite him as an authority."
As for those called "sages" (shengren), who among those in the world would follow them? The Master said: "Wen Zhongzi was a refined Confucian.

Had he been able to assist Emperor Taizong, his governance would surely have been no less than that of the Three Dynasties. Since his office was in charge of compiling the history, he must have certainly ranked the Buddha and Laozi among the sages.
Formerly, when Chen Shuda compiled the History of Sui, he avoided taking sides with the contemporary [rulers], whereas Sima Qian—"
I have composed a biography to supplement it. That Tu Mu concealed this talent and failed to recommend him—how could that be the public mind of the world?
Pi Rixiu said that Mencius and Xun Qing assisted in transmitting the Way of Confucius; as for Wenzhongzi, Sima Kuang said: [and so forth].

Heaven bestowed Wen Zhongzi so that the utility of the Sage could be realized. Thus, figures such as Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui expanded upon the principles of Wen and Wu to bring about the governance of the Zhenguan era;
through these achievements, one is fully able to understand Wen Zhongzi.

Conversely, followers of Xun Qing, such as Han Fei, prioritized the doctrine of "form and name" (xingming) to harm the world, while Li Si burned the *Odes* and *Documents* to bring ruin to Qin. The calamity caused by Yang Zhu and Mo Di was likewise... [uncompleted].
It comes to this: were not the disciples of Wenzhongzi able to assist the Tang dynasty in achieving governance through the Way of benevolence and righteousness?
As for Yang Xiong and Han Yu, they merely established empty words; we hear of no disciples of theirs who achieved the merit of assisting in the rise of the Han or the prosperity of the Tang.
Thus, was not the Way of Wenzhongzi superior to that of Xunzi, Yangzi, and Hanzi? And yet—
"Are scholars of later generations not aware of this? Xiu said: 'In the Way of Master Han (Han Yu), there is little that does not accord with that of Master Wen (Wen Zhongzi).
Had he encountered Emperor Taizong, he would surely have fully developed his latent potential. The Master said: 'Emperor Xianzong was a sovereign who restored the dynasty.
Yet when Tu-ji [Han Yu] was at court, he did not offer any assistance or counsel; instead, he took the refutation of Buddhism and Daoism as his own achievement.'"
He wishes to compare himself to Mencius’s refutation of Yang Zhu and Mo Di; his desire for victory and the acquisition of fame is so extreme.
Furthermore, regarding Han Yu’s denunciation of the Buddha as a foreign ghost, I shall briefly examine this. The Buddha, a sage, descended from the Tuṣita Heaven.
He took birth into the family of a holy king in Central India. Why, then, do you call him a "barbarian" (*yi*)? The Buddha, a holy man, is neither born nor extinguished;
he has existed eternally through vast kalpas as the object of veneration for devas and humans. Why, then, do you call him a "ghost" (*gui*)?

Is this not the great arrogance of one who has fallen from his station? Tuizhi’s seventh-generation ancestor, Han Qi, during the Yongxing era of the Later Wei, came to surrender from the rule of Helian Chucai.

The Tuoba [clan] descended from the Western Rong and returned to the Northern Di; they alone did not observe the taboo against mentioning their own ancestors' names, yet how dare they venture to slander the Buddha, the Sage?
Han Yu feared the consequences of praise and censure in historical writing, yet he failed to consider that his own act of slandering the Buddha was even more fearsome.
He took it upon himself to expel Laozi [from the canon], yet he treated Mao Xian as an elder brother, ingested his elixir, and ultimately died of a carbuncle that broke out [as a result].
Zi-chang was unskilled at proofreading; he was ultimately dismissed and returned home, and within a few generations his lineage was extinguished.
Was this not because one cannot escape the punishments of Heaven or the calamities of men? You, Mr. Tu, have advocated the exclusion of Buddhism and Daoism, and you now join me in this.
Will you not cause future scholars who prize their reputations to take the houses of Han (Mencius) and Ouyang (Xunzi) as their models? Would this not be a matter of great virtue?
This is a source of reproach. There is a proverb that says: "He who excels at reviling will himself be reviled by others.

You have long authored the *Benlun* (On the Origin of Things), diligently making it your task to disparage the Buddha. How could you expect the multitude not to disparage you before the hearing of Heaven?

As for your words, you consider the rites of hunting, mourning, sacrifices, and the archery of the countryside to be superior; yet you treat the fundamental teachings of the Buddha as if they were inferior to those of Han Yu.
He began by speaking of the Way, yet in truth he did not yet understand it. Liu Xiu was greatly startled and ashamed, and apologized, saying, "My mind has already been set at ease;
what further instruction could you possibly give me? The Master said, "The Buddha-way takes the awakening of the mind as its foundation.

You have realized the Way through many lifetimes, yet you merely lost mindfulness. Having been born in Donghua as a renowned Confucian scholar, you became biased toward worldly teachings and thus forgot your original nature."

If one can truly employ a mind of equality toward both the holy and the ordinary, silently experiencing this realization, suddenly casting off self-conceit (*māna*), and fully repenting for past errors;

if one contemplates that honor and disgrace are fundamentally empty and understands that death and life are of one essence, then pure mindfulness will become clear and the original nature (*tianzhen*) will be uniquely revealed.
Only then may one begin to inquire into the path of this Way. From this point on, Xiuxi experienced considerable awakening and insight, and subsequently entered...
He participated in high state affairs and frequently praised [the Buddha] before the dukes and ministers. His seasonal inquiries and correspondence never ceased.

Regarding the *Fofa jintang bian* (The Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Fortress): During the Xining era, Lord Lü served as the Governor of Henan; during the Yuanyou era, he served alongside Wen Gong as Grand Councillor.
He served four successive emperors, was enfeoffed as Duke of Shen, and was posthumously titled Zhengxian. In his later years, he read many Buddhist scriptures with increasing devotion.

He investigated the principles of Chan and ritual. Lord Wen did not favor Buddhism, yet the Master (Fan Zhongyan) would frequently advise him, saying, "The Buddhist teachings are simple and essential in their core method.
If one extracts and understands these most vital points, they generally take the rectification of the mind and non-conceptualization as their foundation. Lord Wen agreed with this.
During the Xining era, when Wang Anshi implemented the Green Sprouts Law, his son Wang Pang served as a Lecturer at the Chongzheng Hall.

Yang Yin served as his father’s assistant in state affairs, and the new laws were certain to be implemented. Upon Yang Ping’s death, the Duke (Ouyang Xiu) was also dismissed from the相位 (prime ministership). During a period of leisure and seclusion, he experienced a vision exactly like a dream:

he saw an official leading Yang Ping, who was shackled with an iron cangue, weeping and wailing before him. The messenger said, "Your son has incurred this retribution because of the implementation of the Qingmiao (Green Sprouts) law.

The Duke asked the messenger for a way to secure his release. The messenger replied, "Building a temple and providing a vegetarian feast for the monks can exempt him. Thereupon, [the Duke] made donations.
He established a temple at his residence to dedicate merit for the deceased. In the eighth year of the Xining era, the Duke was once again appointed as Chancellor.

One day, after retiring from a court audience, the Emperor asked, "Does the Buddha-dharma provide any benefit to the Middle Kingdom? The Duke replied, "Both the noble and the common people know to stand in awe and follow what is good;
how could this be anything less than a great benefit?"
From the *Zhupō Shìhuà*: Guān Zīdōng of Qiāntáng told me that during the Xīníng era, there was an elder named Chóngxǐ, a native of Huìjī.
In his youth, he made his living by fishing; nevertheless, he recited the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva every day without ceasing for even a moment.
Originally illiterate, one day he was suddenly able to write and could also compose verses and hymns. He once composed a verse that said: "The hearth has no fire, my single bag is empty;
The snow falls like willow blossoms as the year draws to its end. I have begged for ramie to sew together this tattered robe; I do not know that I am standing in the midst of solitude.
How could such a person, who was once a fisherman, have been capable of this? His realization was of such a caliber. Indeed...
This is to attain the power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom.
According to the *Qingxiang zajiji*, Duke Chen Wenhui realized the principles of nature and reason. Once, while visiting an ancient temple, he composed a verse, saying:
"The hall is ancient, the incense burner cold and empty; Dust flows, obscuring the gold and green. Sitting alone, by chance there is no one; Thus I have received the true message."

The Duke of Wenzhong, Fu, was profoundly adept in the principles of human nature and destiny (*xingli*). During the Xining era, when I was serving as an official in Luoyang, the Duke was then the Governor of Bozhou.
He sent me a letter requesting that I seek out images of various Chan masters from Heze. I therefore playfully addressed him with a verse: [Verse follows]
This body is like a bubble or a phantom; in its entirety, it lacks any mark of reality. How much more so this shadow upon paper—a delusion arising from delusion.
Once the shore is reached, the boat is unnecessary; when there is no wind, the waves cease. One should simply practice pure observation: the wondrous Dharma is ultimately without form.
The Duke replied with a verse: "To cling to marks is truly false; to negate marks is likewise delusive. Neither clinging nor negating—this is called the true mark.
He then further sent me a letter by hand, saying: "I have received this verse and am alerted by it. While it is indeed elegant, its principle is not yet correct.
Regarding what is called 'neither can nor cannot,' one may paint, or one may not paint; one should contemplate within that state."
As for the image, it is not attained. As for not contemplating the image, what is attained? Where does dhyāna reside?
If it seems that existence and non-existence do not constitute an obstacle, one is close to penetration. Think on this, think on this!
In the *Bishu Luhua* (Records of Avoiding the Heat), it is noted that Fan Chengda of Shu was by nature a non-drinker and moreover disparaged Buddhism.
While residing in Xuzhou, he maintained close relations with the Han brothers, including Han Chigu; yet all the Hans were great admirers of these two matters [drinking and Buddhism].

At every banquet gathering, Fan never failed to drink to his heart’s content and enjoy himself to the fullest. When the occasion allowed for a brief interval, he would invariably urge them to discuss Chan. Fan Chengda grew somewhat weary of this.
Su Zizhan was at that time in Huangzhou; he sent a letter inquiring how to save him. [The reply] said: "The yeast and malt have poison growing on level ground;
one has emerged from the Land of the Drunken, where earthen figurines act as malevolent spirits. What appears before one's eyes is a delusory vision of the Buddha-land."

I looked at him and replied: "Please allow me to observe this for you. From what source does the nature that is capable of delusion arise? What form or appearance does the mind that seeks to save take?
If even this [deluded nature] is not established, upon what can that [mind of salvation] rely? I fear that even the Yellow-Faced Gautama must fold his robes in respect;
how much more so for those who merely study his teachings? Although I intended to clarify this for him, he ultimately did not understand. Furthermore—
It can be seen that he was firm in his faith and self-restraint, refusing to be swayed by external things.
This continues from the *Mingdao zazhi*. Lord Fan of Shu did not believe in Buddhist teachings.

Once, Lord Su of Da engaged in a discussion on the Buddha-dharma with him, interrogating him regarding the reasons for his lack of belief. Lord Fan said, "Throughout my life’s affairs, I have accepted nothing that has not been witnessed by my own eyes."
[The interlocutor] replied, "I have never believed it. Su Gong said, "How could you possibly do so? Suppose you were ill and ordered a physician to examine your pulse.
If the physician said it was cold, you would take hot medicine; if he said it was hot, you would ingest cold medicine.
When have you ever actually seen the pulse, yet do you believe it so completely? Why then, when it comes to the Buddha alone, must you insist on seeing him?"
From *Dongpo Zhilin*: Zhuo Chishun, a temple attendant at the Dinghui Monastery on Mount Su, traveled several thousand li, crossing ridges and seas, to inquire after the well-being of Dongpo.
Dongpo asked, "What local products have you brought? Chishun extended both hands. Dongpo said, "What a pity!
To come from thousands of li with empty hands. Chishun assumed the posture of carrying a burden and strode away.
Upon leaving, Tanxiu came to Huizhou to see Su Shi. As he was about to depart, Su Shi said, "When you return from the mountains and see you, he will surely ask for something.
What shall I give him? Tanxiu replied, "The pure breeze of Goose City and the bright moon of Crane Ridge—everyone can offer these;
I only fear he may have no place to put them. Su Shi said, "It would be better to take some sheets of paper with you and give one to each person."
One sheet of paper. He simply said: "This is the Dharma; within these written words lie calamity and fortune.
The Stone Pagoda came to bid farewell to东坡 (Dongpo). Dongpo said, "I have been traveling in haste; I regret not having met you, Stone Pagoda. The Pagoda stood up and said:
Zha said, "Is this a brick stupa? Su Shi replied, "It is a stupa with seams. Zha said, "If it were seamless, how could it accommodate the ants of the world?
Su Shi nodded his head in agreement.
Xian Yi, the Supervisor of Jinnan, Song Baoguo, brought out the Master of Jing’s commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for inspection.

Dongpo asked, "The *Avataṃsaka* consists of eighty-one fascicles; why is only this one here? Baoguo replied, "Your Excellency says that these words are the most profound and subtle speech of the Buddha, while all others are merely the words of Bodhisattvas.
Dongpo said, "I shall select the words of the Buddha from within the Tripitaka myself."

[Suppose someone] takes several phrases from among the words of a Bodhisattva and mixes them with those of a Buddha, or takes several phrases from among the words of a Buddha and mixes them with those of a Bodhisattva—could you distinguish which is which?
He replied, "I could not. Dongpo said: "In the past, when I was under Qifu, I heard that the pork of Heyang was exceptionally fine.
I sent a messenger to purchase some. The messenger became drunk, and the pig escaped in the night. He then bought another pig to pay for the debt."

The guests were all greatly astonished, believing that no other product could surpass it. Shortly thereafter, the matter fell through, and the guests were all ashamed. Now, Lord Jing’s pigs have not yet failed;
however, if one’s single thought is pure, even walls, fences, tiles, and rubble all preach the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma.
To then claim that the Buddha’s words are so profound and subtle that Bodhisattvas cannot reach them—is this not merely the talk of a dream? —Huang.
Once, when Old Man Haitang of Longsi Temple asked Huang Shan谷 (Shangu) for the meaning of the passage, "I have nothing hidden from you," Shangu explained it to him repeatedly;
yet Haitang ultimately did not accept his interpretation. At that time, the summer heat had subsided and a cool breeze arose, as the fragrance of autumn flowers filled the courtyard.
Hui asked, "Is the osmanthus fragrant? Huangbo (Shan谷) replied, "I smell it. Huitang said, "I have hidden nothing from you. Huangbo then submitted to this.
Later, Minister Han Zonggu sent a letter to Huitang, asking: "In the past, I heard that when you, Master, attained awakening, you were vast and free of doubt.
However, since beginningless time, the habitual tendencies of affliction (*kleśa-vāsanā*) have not yet been completely exhausted."
Huitang said: "There is no dharma remaining outside the mind. Not knowing what these afflictions and habitual tendencies are, you wish to exhaust them.

From the time of the ancient sages until now, all verbal teachings have been medicines prescribed according to the illness. If there were truly habitual tendencies to be treated, it would be like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail through the mud;
as soon as one tries to wipe away the tracks, new tracks are produced. This can be called 'using the mind to employ the mind,' which only serves to increase the delusion."

The insight into the illness is profound. If one clearly understands that there is no phenomenon outside the mind and no mind outside phenomena, and since both mind and phenomena are non-existent, whom else would one wish to instruct in order to bring about their sudden exhaustion?
From the *Manxiao lu* (Record of Idle Laughter): When Chan Master Foyin ascended the seat for Wang Guanwen, he said:

"This single offering of incense is for the Doctor Who Sweeps Away Smoke and Dust, the Great King Who Protects the World, the Generalissimo Who Kills Men Without Blinking His Eyes—the Great Layman, Duke Wang, who has attained Buddhahood on the spot.
Wang was greatly pleased, though it was because his long-standing service as a military commander had been primarily devoted to killing.
From the *Wenjian jilu* (Records of What I Have Heard and Seen): A monk from Xianping County possessed a single Buddha-tooth relic, about two finger-widths in size and pale gold in color.
I once requested it for veneration; in an instant, śarīra beads emerged from within the tooth.

At first they were like dewdrops, moving along the surface of the tooth or traveling as far as several dozen paces. Those who sought them invariably obtained them. I requested forty-eight grains, wishing to seek more.
It was intended to be forty-nine grains, yet after spending the night, they could not be found. When the casket was opened the next day, the number was already complete.
Furthermore, some said that there were grains which emerged from the Cave of Ambrosia (Ganlu). The next day he went again to request them, but obtained none.

He then traveled more than ten li beyond the gate of Chenzhou to seek them, but still obtained none. Consequently, he prostrated himself and took his leave to return; as he rose from his prostration, one grain appeared.
It emerged from the Cave of Ambrosia (*amṛta*), its size like that of a mung bean, its radiance brilliant.
Later, Emperor Shenzong welcomed it into the imperial palace and eventually returned it, sealed within a casket. Nowadays, few people have the opportunity to see it. Shi Chaolinglin stated:
while serving as a Vice Prefect in Xuzhou, the wife’s wet nurse of the Regional Commander Guo Yuming paid homage to the stupa for several years.
As the period of his ritual observances was nearing its end, he had been using *yiyi* seeds to count them. Suddenly, the *yiyi* seeds leaped from their container;
looking at them, he saw *śarīra* relics filling the space before him, all emerging from within the *yiyi* seeds. He obtained several spoonfuls in total.

A moment later, within the silver stupa where he was performing worship, a brilliant spiritual light shone forth and *śarīra* fell like rain. Shortly thereafter, *śarīra* appeared on both knees of his wet nurse.

Countless times he prostrated before the stupa, yet the relics remained hidden and painful to behold. For several days, his mother exerted herself with unwavering diligence until the location of the stupa was lost.
He recorded this in a note. Later, while serving as the Inspector of Shanwu in Dingping, he passed by the Sengqie Stupa at Sizhou and composed a text of vows.
He abstained from alcohol, sexual indulgence, and meat, eating only morning gruel and a midday meal, in accordance with the dharma of the *buddhaputra*.
In the *Lengzhai Yehua*, Chen Liaoweng reproached me for being improper, calling me "Ganlu Mie" (Extinction of Sweet Dew) a recent and insolent title.
He said: "The one who attains 'the extinction of sweet dew' and achieves the Way of Awakening is the Tathāgata’s consciousness. You, a commoner, are merely looking up to or down at my kind;

the distance between you and the Buddha-ground is like that between heaven and an abyss. How can you presume upon such a magnificent name and claim it as your own? To this, I replied: [The text continues with the author's response.]
It is said: "To say that I cannot be called 'the extinction of ambrosia' (*amṛta-nirvāṇa*) is like saying honey cannot be called sweet, or gold cannot be called yellow in color.
The World-Honored One, through great skillful means (*upāya*), enlightens all sentient beings so that they may know the fundamental reality;
