Fahai replied, "Taiping Hongfu and Guoqing Wannian. The Emperor said, "I have heard that Shiqiao Ying is truly one of the five hundred [arhats]."

A powerful Han [official] suddenly appeared at that time. "By what means do you deal with him? [the Emperor asked]. Mao clenched his fist and said, "Your servant possesses the Vajra-king Precious Sword.
The Sovereign was pleased and bestowed upon him the title "Old Man Suichu."

*The Record of Heavenly Destiny*. Wang Chuchu, courtesy name Yuanshi, was a native of Huayang County in Yizhou. Once he encountered an elderly monk who discussed with him the matters of suffering and emptiness in this floating world.
After passing the imperial examinations and serving as a provincial official, he wandered along ancient roads; moved by deep emotion, he composed this long chant: [Text follows]

Who says that matters of past and present are inexhaustible? For the most part, both prosperity and decay are entirely empty. One may calculate that life before death follows the dream of the butterfly, yet how can this compare to pointing toward the soaring wild geese beyond the clouds?
The color of snow secretly adds whiteness to the roots of one's brows; the falling flower-light momentarily flushes the face with red.
In sorrow at the desolate wilderness, I am loath to turn my head back; from the withered woods at twilight, a mournful wind arises. At dusk, he returned home.
His heart failed and he passed away.
According to the *Jin shi* (History of Jin), Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong, in the first month of the eighth year of Dading, the Emperor said to Yila Zijung and others of the Secretariat:
"Regarding the Buddha-dharma, I have particularly little faith. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty became a slave at Tongtai Temple; the Liao [Emperor Dao...]"
The Emperor bestowed the households of commoners upon the temple monks and further conferred upon them the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers; how deep was his delusion!
The *Yuanshi*, in the biography of Soga, records that Soga’s son, Hulian, was of exceptionally sincere character, yet he was also a fervent devotee of Buddhism.
He once expended ten thousand taels of gold to repair Longgong Temple and established a Great Golden Wheel Assembly, providing offerings for ten thousand monks.
*Chuēgēnglù* (Records of Ceasing Plow Work). The emperors of successive dynasties first receive the Buddhist precepts before ascending the great throne.
When assuming the position of Great Treasure, there must be nine attendants in attendance, or seven; these are called *nuǎndá* by the interpreters. This is the custom of this country.
At the beginning of the present sovereign’s reign, when entering the ordination platform (*jiètán*), he saw an object serving as an offering before the Mahā Buddha. Consequently...
The Emperor asked the scholar Saraban, "What is this? He replied, "It is a sheep’s heart. The Emperor said, "I have heard that there are those who use human hearts and livers.
Saraban replied, "I have heard of such things, but I have never seen them with my own eyes. [The Emperor] then requested that Saralam—the Imperial Preceptor (Ti-shi)—be questioned.
The Emperor subsequently ordered Saraban to transmit his command to him. Saralam replied, "There are indeed such cases. When ordinary people give rise to..."
"One who harbors a wicked intent to harm others shall, upon their crime being discovered, have their heart and liver used as an offering.
When he reported this again, the Emperor asked once more, "Has this sheep ever harmed anyone? The Imperial Preceptor (Ti-shi) had no answer.

One day, Se-zu (Shizu) commanded the upright Wang Lian to receive the precepts from the National Preceptor (Guo-shi). Wang replied, "Your Majesty, I have already received the precepts of Confucius. The Emperor—
The Emperor asked, "Does your Confucius also have precepts? He replied, "As a minister one should be loyal; as a son one should be filial.
Such are the precepts of the school of Confucius. The Emperor was pleased. During the Zhizhen era of the Yuan dynasty, the followers of Śākyamuni became arrogant and overbearing.

They converted palaces and shrines into Buddhist temples and forcibly shaved the heads of Daoist priests. Furthermore, they excavated nearly all the imperial tombs in various locations. At this time, Lin He of Gushan...
The tomb of Recluse Jing was empty; the remains were entirely gone, leaving behind only a single jade hairpin. At that time, someone composed a poem in lamentation for him, which said:
"In life he did not fasten a golden girdle; after death, there remains only an empty white jade hairpin.

Now, when the current Emperor’s Crown Prince ascends to his rightful position in the Eastern Palace, the office of *Yude* (Counselor for Virtue) is established and the *Duanbentang* (Hall for Cultivating the Root) is set up to attend to the Crown Prince.

During his studies, one day the Imperial Preceptor arrived and addressed the Crown Prince’s mother and the Empress Dowager, saying: "Previously, the Crown Prince studied the Buddha-dharma and suddenly attained awakening.
Now, however, you have caused him to practice the teachings of Confucius; I fear this may corrupt the Prince's true nature. The Empress Dowager replied:
"Though I dwell within the secluded palace, I am not ignorant of morality. I have often heard that from antiquity until now, those who have governed the world..."
"One must employ the Way of Confucius; to abandon this and seek elsewhere is to become a heterodox sect.

Although the Buddha-dharma is excellent, it is merely a secondary matter and cannot be used to govern the world. How could one allow the Crown Prince not to study? The Imperial Preceptor, feeling ashamed, withdrew.
During the Dade era, there was a monk named Danba whom all the officials of the court at that time revered for his virtue.
The Crown Prince fell ill and passed away at Banrong Buluhan. The Empress sent someone to inquire, saying, "My husband and I have revered the Buddha-dharma and have served you as our teacher.
We have but this one son; could you not have prolonged his life? He replied, "The Buddha-dharma is like a lantern.
When wind and rain arrive, it can be shielded; but once the candle is spent, there is nothing that can be done."
*Fófǎjīntángbiān*. Liù Guàn, courtesy name Dàotuán, was a native of Dōngyáng. He once served as a *tàicháng bóshì*.

He composed a preface to the *Yŭlù* (Recorded Sayings) of Master Zhú Yuándào, which states in brief: "Chan has its strategic mechanisms (*jī*), and military arts have their methods (*fǎ*). Therefore, discussing Chan is like employing troops;

one must reach the point where guest and host respond to one another, such that both trace and function are simultaneously extinguished. Only then does one forget the dharma and realize the dharma. Forgetting... [text ends].
The resonance of the spiritual affinity is sublime, wondrous, perfect, and luminous; it is beyond the need for further words.

The *Record of the Western Regions* mentions a Buddhist kingdom named Qishimixi (Kashmir), located to the northwest of India. It is there that the dharma-robes and alms bowl of Śākyamuni were transmitted.
The people there possess very ancient features, resembling the images of Bodhidharma depicted in the world, and they do not consume pungent herbs or meat.
She abstained from alcohol and consumed only one *he* of non-glutinous rice daily. All she discussed was the Buddha-dharma.
The *Yaqing ji* records that in her later years, Lady Zhang refrained from eating meat and recited the name of Amitābha every day.
Her family members all laughed at her, saying, "An elderly person should simply focus on nourishing and sustaining herself with tonics; to be so diligent as this will likely do more harm than good."

The lady practiced this with ever-increasing devotion. At the age of seventy-nine, every night in the darkness she saw four walls draped in *śroṇī-koṭi* (necklaces), their radiance illuminating people so vividly it was as if it were broad daylight.
As she approached her end, she burned incense upon her desk; the smoke curled and coiled until it formed a small image of Amitābha.
At first it was the color of smoke, then it gradually turned a pale yellow, finally becoming the color of true gold, its features—eyebrows and eyes—as distinct as life.
A painting [was made] with one hand hanging down, like the present-day sculpted image of the Guiding Buddha (Jielin). The assembly all prostrated themselves and recited the Buddha’s name.
As soon as the smoke and the image vanished, the Lady drew her last breath. Ying Yuan visited the Yuan school extensively but found nothing at all there.
One day, Yingyuan went to visit Master Wuxin and asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "A mindless state is the Buddha. Yingyuan said, "Brother, lend me ten days;
within that time I shall become a Buddha. If I do not, I am no longer Yingyuan. Having returned home, he lamented his own dull faculties.
He secluded himself in a single room; whenever a thought arose, he would immediately pinch the flesh of his own arm until the flesh was completely exhausted.
Blood flowed from his body, and his discursive thoughts diminished daily. On the tenth day, amidst heavy rain and lightning, he was suddenly illuminated by a flash of light;
his thoughts were severed, and there was no mind to be found. He then attained enlightenment. Upon awakening, Yunguan shouted, "A mindless state is not the Buddha!
At these words, Yuan attained great enlightenment. When people examined his arms, they found not a single intact patch of skin remaining.

*Da zheng ji* (Great Record of Government). The fifth month of the fifth year of the Yongle era, on the day *guiyou*. The Sovereign discussed with his attendants the contemporary custom of venerating the Buddha while neglecting the ancestors.
The Sovereign said to his attendants: "I have heard that among the current customs, there is a tendency to be rigorous in serving the Buddha while being negligent toward one's ancestors;
is this indeed the case? They replied: "There are instances of it. The Sovereign sighed and said: "This is surely due to the failure of moral instruction (*jiaohua*)."
This is the fault of ignorance. At the Fengxian Hall, I pay my respects morning and evening, never daring to be disrespectful;

even when I am slightly unwell, I exert myself to perform the rites. That people exhaust their efforts to venerate the Buddhas and Laozi while treating the rites at the Fengxian Hall with negligence is because they are mired in the doctrine of fortune and misfortune and have lost sight of the fundamental. I shall lead them by correcting this.
"It must indeed begin with me. This is recorded in the *Mingtongji*.
In the twelfth month of the ninth year of Xuande, a monk came forward and stated that he wished to solicit offerings to repair a temple and pray for the prolongation of the Emperor's life.
The Emperor rebuked him. After the court session had concluded, he turned to his attendants and said, "In human nature, there is none who does not desire—"
Longevity: Among the ancient rulers, such as Shang’s Zhongzong, Gaozong, and Zu Jia, as well as King Wen of Zhou, all enjoyed their reigns for an exceedingly long duration.
In their time, how could there have been monks or Daoists? How could there have been talk of transcendents? It was only the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han who sought after transcendents.

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty revered monks and Daoists; the efficacy [of their devotion] is clearly visible. Yet the people of this world never awaken to this truth—how deeply lamentable!

In the *Yingya Shenglüan* (A Survey of the Great Oceans), it is recorded that in the country of Xiyang, there was a copper mold for Buddha images called the "Nārī Buddha Hall," which featured a copper-tiled pedestal.
Beside [the temple], they dig wells and draw spring water to bathe the Buddha and pay him homage. They take cow dung mixed with water to smear upon the ground and the walls.
Ministers, subjects, and members of great families also rise at dawn and likewise smear their floors with cow dung. They carry bags of cow-dung ash on their persons;
every morning, they mix the ash with water and smear it upon their foreheads and thighs, which is called "revering the Buddha."

In the *Xù Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo* (Continued Comprehensive Examination of Literary Contributions), it is recorded that Zhou Wenxiang Gong (Zhou Chen) was by nature fond of Buddhism. While serving as the Viceregent (Xunfu) of the Wu region, he would stroll leisurely through Buddhist monasteries;
wherever he went, the sounds of temple bells and drums followed one another. Upon entering a Buddha hall, he would prostrate himself in deep reverence. Some people mocked him for this.
The Duke said, "If we were to judge by age alone, he is indeed my senior; both of us are two or three thousand years old.
How could I not offer him one or two bows? Yet he continued his practice as before, without change.
There was a monk named Xianyi who lived his life reciting sutras without ceasing. A disciple of his traveled abroad to seek enlightenment and, upon returning, reflected upon his master.
One day, pointing to a window lattice, he asked a fly, "Hey! Why do you not soar toward the vast expanse of space, but instead wallow day after day, boring into this old paper?
How will you ever emerge? At these words, his master attained realization.
An Examination of Buddhist Training: The Qi Zhongmin Gong family had followed the Buddhist path for generations;

they donated their residence to become a temple, and both brothers followed the Elder Yuan’an to greatly propagate the teachings that came from the West. The Duke’s name was Biu; he died as a loyal minister according to his word.
Li Guo was a man of talent and literary ability, yet he was fundamentally unimpressed by Buddhism and had no liking for Mencius; he was fond of wine and fine food.
One day, an official of high rank sent several *dou* of wine. At that time, Taibo’s own home-brewed wine was also ready.
A certain scholar, knowing that [Taibo] possessed plenty of wine but having no means to obtain some to drink, composed several poems in which he reviled Mencius.

One of them said: "Whether the granary was completed or the steps damaged remains uncertain; Mencius’s deep faith is likewise nothing but folly. The father-in-law is currently serving as the Son of Heaven."
The son-in-law asked, "How did you kill your younger brother? When Li saw this, he was greatly pleased and stayed for several days.
In all his conversations, there was nothing but the reviling of Mencius. Before long, the wine ran out, so he took his leave. Shortly thereafter, he heard that someone else had sent him wine.
The scholar went again and composed three essays on Benevolence and Righteousness (*Ren-yi Zheng-lun*), which for the most part all reviled the followers of Śākyamuni.
When Li saw them, he laughed and said, "Your literary talent is truly extraordinary; however, last time you were so intoxicated by your wine that you became utterly despondent afterward.
This time I dare not detain you, but I shall leave this wine here to dispel your melancholy. Those who heard this burst into laughter.
Chan Master Quanzi arrived in Xunjiang carrying his alms bowl. Mr. Luo Jinxī received him with great reverence.
After several years had passed, the Master took his leave one day. Jinxī grasped his hand and requested, "Master, out of your compassion, as we part now, I pray for a word to aid me.
The Master replied, "There is nothing to say to you, sir. You, a man of official standing, always possess a fine radiance."
"Jing, there are favorable conditions, and there are also unfavorable conditions; they all await me. A renunciant is exactly like this.
When Jinxi heard this, he suddenly attained realization and prostrated himself on the ground several dozen times to express his gratitude.
*Da zheng ji* (Great Record of State Affairs). The eighth day of the fourth month in the fourteenth year of the Jiajing era, *yiwei*.
Initially following the teachings of the Buddhists, the Emperor granted food to his ministers on this day, serving it without the use of chopsticks (*bualuo jia*).

The Emperor, finding the name of the practice unrefined, ordered that fresh wheat be offered in the inner palace on the fifth day, whereupon wheat cakes were made and served to the ministers. From then on, this was established as an annual custom.
*Record of Extraordinary Objects from Various Temples*. At Tianjie Temple there is a Buddha’s tooth, one *cun* wide and five times that length.
During the Wanli era, the monk Zhenchun presented it to Minister Lu of Wutai.

The Minister consequently prepared a golden casket and a sandalwood shrine to enshrine it, and invited it to be worshipped in the Vairocana Hall of the temple. This tooth was obtained from Mount Tiantai.

The Gazetteer of Jiaxing Prefecture records that during the Wanli era, there was a woman named Chang, the daughter of Hu Rihu of the Imperial Academy, who became a chaste widow at the age of nineteen.
Behind the Yueshan Nunnery, she constructed the Cixiao Hall to provide for her parents, where she lived together with nuns to practice Buddhist cultivation.
